Deadlight is a platform puzzler set in a 1960's Seattle after some sort of an apocalyptic event that turned people into "shadows" (i.e. Zombies). You pay Randall Wayne, forest ranger, nature lover, and survivalist, and you are determined to do what is necessary to save your family from any threat, be it human or Shadow...  While gunplay is possible, it is discouraged, as ammo is extremely limited (you can carry less than 20 rounds of each ammo, and you rarely find more). Your other weapons are even MORE limited in utility. So you need to RUN from the Shadows usually, and/or finding a way to go where they can't (fortunately, they can't climb ladders).
You start alone, as the group you hung with chose to strike out on their own. You try to make your way to the safe zone, hoping for safety there, and perhaps, your family. The game will have you doing a bit of Prince of Persia jumps as you jump from ledge to ledge, ladder to overhead pipe, leaping over barbed wired topped storm fences, doing wall leap  (reach higher spot than normal jump by pushing off the opposite wall) , crouch in pipes, over cars... The game is 2D but has parallax and perspective scrolling to give the illusion of 3D. The players and other objects are full 3D, and nicely animated.
As with all platformers, frustration set in when you tried to repeat the same segment 15-20 times and could get past it, as you need to repeat a sequence back exactly timed or you fail. Leap here, leap again there, reverse aim here, forward, climb a fence but not jump off, shoot enemies, etc.  That's a pretty long sequence lasting minutes, and there are no savepoints in between so you're forced to repeat the whole thing should you fail. The infamous "helicopter sequence" here needs no explanation.
There are a ton of collectible objects in the game for you to find, if you like that sort of item hunting.
All in all, Deadlight is an action puzzler set in a unique era and thus achieves something remarkable: making a zombie game interesting again. If you like the idea of a different zombie game, get this game.
NOTE: Best played with a gamepad, such as the Xbox360 controller. You don't really want to play with keyboard . Also, ALT-Tab performance is occasional freeze-ups), loses sound in the cutscenes, and few minor bugs.

I like the idea of this game. You are part of a group of survivors in yet another zombie apocalypse. It's something of a cross between Left 4 Dead and a survival game, without the sandbox aspect.
The atmosphere is fairly good. I also welcome the randomization to the maps. The visuals and sounds are okay, except it's a bit difficult to orient yourself by sound alone. Sadly, the experience tends to be very boring.
First of all, it takes a long time to finish the missions. The things you have to do to proceed doesn't always seem to make a lot of sense, and you'll have to search around the map trying to figure it out. It is particularly frustrating to join a game already in progress, trying to find your teammated in the giant maze. You're equipped with a cellphone that receives messages when progress advances, explaining somewhat what to do, but figuring out where the place is located is is another matter.
Lastly, playing as a zombie downright sucks. If you get bitten, you change sides, meaning you should try to kill the team you were part of. Attacking as a zombie is.. an unsatisfying experience and feels very clunky.
The game is overall unfinished and unsatisfying. Even though there are some nice concepts in there, I simply cannot recommend it at this time.
2014.04.15: The game recently had its official release. The game is a bit more polished now and there are new maps. However, most of the time the game is still plain boring. It's hard to find your teammates when you join an existing game. Playing as a zombie is as boring as can be, again much because you have to search for the other players. Lastly, sometimes it's just impossible, or seemingly so, to pass on to the next area. I still can't recommend it, especially with the high price tag it has.
2014.10.02: I've decided to flip my review in slight favor now. It's better than it used to be. Things have gotten fixed and there is at least one more map. It's a bit rough still though.
2015.01.15: More maps and modes have been added eventually. Some of the levels look really nice, considering it's running on the Source engine and is an "indie" game. It doesn't feel all that great, but it's a decent game.

After about 10 minutes of playing this gamemode, I'm already searching for a server that has players on it that has the FANTASTIC Hunter gamemode! Escape is basically an order of events like a play or drama that you MUST FOLLOW EVERY TIME. And, even worse, there's only ONE MAP! Now, onto that great Hunter gamemode! Hunter is where not only are you trying to kill all the zombies after you, BUT YOU ALSO CAN KILL PLAYERS! :D This mode gets REALLY FUN when you encounter other players. You might need a Mic and turn on your VoiceChat option before you play this or face getting murdered the very second someone sees you. >:)
Now, onto this game's weaknesses. The BIG THING is Escape mode! IT'S BORING! After you've played it once, you'll most likely be reluctant to play it again, even with friends! Overall, this gamemode gets a 5.5/10 for me. Another weakness is some sounds are NON-EXISTANT! xD For example, when I call a hoarde of zombies to my location(to do this press R), there's a cool animation, BUT NO SOUND! LOL The final weakness I have to say about this game is NOT ENOUGH DIVERSITY IN ZOMBIES. There are only(I think) 7 types of zombies! D: So, after a while, you learn the abilities of all the zombies and can usually predict what they are going to do. Now, the AI does mix up stuff every so often, but it's not enough to give the zombies enough diversity to make them COMPLETELY unpredictable.

With almost 500 hours in this game and probably another 500 hours more that will come in the second one, I feel like I can finally review it.
M&B: Warband is unique in so many ways, you truly just start with few gold and some weapons that's it. From there you have to build your way to take over the world. Which is not as easy as it sounds.
There isn't much of a story in this game. Everything said above is pretty much it, it lets you create and do what you want in the game world. All you care about is take over the world kill everyone else. How you choose to do so is up to you.
There are small "quests" within the game that will give you exp to level yourself up as well as your army with skills that will benefit either you, your army or your entire kingdom.
This game is not something you buy for amazing graphics or amazing sound, it is a game you buy for its depth and for the fun of leading grand armies to major battles and sieges. I can honestly say after my 460 hours I haven't won the game. Not even once, always made a mistake or didn't capture enough castles or even worse did get too many. It is a game that has a deep connection with the middle and dark ages.
Marry, kill, capture your way to conquer the world.
Mount & Blade will live for a long long time and there are amazing mods all the time that get added to make the game even better. The two important things you should add to get an amazing experience - 
Floris Mod Pack - 
Warband battle size
These two mods make it possible to have battles up to 600 units on both sides and it looks amazing. Seeing your proud army just clash and kill 100´s of other units is fun. They also provide further more depth to the politics and basic gameplay of the game.
All in all M&B: Warband is one of those games that proves that a game doesn't have to be all about graphics/sounds or any flashy flashy stuff, to make a truly unique and amazing experience that will keep you trapped for years.
So if you are looking for a game that will take your soul for 100s of hours grab this game for sure. It is one of my favorites and is really one of those games that is 100% what YOU decide and make of it.

I remeber bying the first CoD many moons ago and remembered it to be one of the greatest FPSs I have ever played. Hands down. From the original CoD to where we are now, the games have been gradually getting worse. There have been up points, WaW and MW2 had their moments, but aside from that it's been pretty crap. -Graphics/lighting/models - Nothing special, in fact some times quite disappointing. Battefield 3 is prettier...and older, think about that.

Sadly, like all CoD games on PC the multiplayer is easily and frequently hacked by people who have just bought CoD to♥♥♥♥♥♥people off. The Infection mode? All in all, Ghosts is decidedly average; nothing sepearting it from anything else except the CoD badge. Compare it to big name games that came out around the same time and it scores below average. This is a traumatic, exhilarating first person experience.
You will brutally murder people with a machete, tear the skin off of wild animals while they're still warm, dig countless bullets out of your body with a knife and crash Jeeps into ancient underground ruins. You will be mauled by sharks, crocodiles, bears and dingos, get maimed and imprisoned multiple times by a lunatic, accidentally trip some serious balls on hallucinogenic shrooms in a cave, and that's just the first hour of the game.
The tropical island that you'll be annihilating with an increasingly powerful arsenal of weaponry also happens to be inhabited purely by idiots and psychopaths. There is not one single pleasant human being to interact with, and everything that anyone says seems like it was hastily written on the back of a Mountain Dew wrapper in between crunch time coding sessions by young interns.
You end up as a severely disturbed dweeb♥♥♥♥♥Rambo who realises that the inconceivable genocide he ends up having committed for the benefit of the ingrate, cretinous indigenous folk has irreversibly sent his sanity down the crapper. The constant intravenous intake of strong narcotics to dull the staggering physical ordeals hasn't helped either. He concedes that he can no longer integrate with human society and must therefore remain far removed from it, much to the complete indifference of his phony, sociopath "friends" he risked life and limb for again and again.
It's a tragic tale, flimsily executed and aspiring to be more than it is, clumsily told and lacking any profound meaning or satisfying conclusion, with plot holes as large as undead bears. But who needs a relatable, engaging narrative when you'll be living vicariously through white 20-something middle-class male juvenile power fantasies blowing up stuff real good and sniping Machiavellian bad guys in the face, all in a gorgeously rendered setting with superbly smooth, crisp controls?
100% still worth playing in 2016.

I first heard about this game through my roommate who studies history.  At first I brushed off the game once I saw single player interactions and it seemed too sandbox-y and outdated for me.  I saw the game on sale for $4.00 and picked it up to try it out and boy it has easily been the best purchase I've ever made.  It is unreal how much entertainment I've recieved through this purchase.  This game is an all-time favorite.  I could put endless hours into it and still keep playing.  The multiplayer is the most solid I've ever experienced because it is so flexible.  You can be a really serious player or you can be a jokester if you prefer.  You can operate alone or in numbers.  You can focus on shooting with your comrades or master melee combat.  You can fight on foot or on cavalry.  You can choose to be a gunner, a musician, an engineer, or an artillery unit with subclasses for many of the unit types listed.  There's so much here to see and do.
While the campaign is also very addicting and often times the sole reason people purchase this game, it is my personal opinion that the single player could be entirely skipped and it would still be worth a purchase.  You will laugh, you will cheer, you will get frustrated, and you'll be surprised by the small improvements you make in understanding the mechanics of all the systems the game has to offer.
The Napoleonic Wars DLC is ESSENTIAL for this game.  I almost exclusively play the game through Napoleonic Wars.  There is something SO satisfying about a successful hit using an inaccurate primitive firearm.  If the era and battle style intrigue you enough you might consider joining a regiment and engage in organized 200 person line battles!
This game has TONS of wonderful mods, TONS of active communities, TONS of replayability, and Tons of mechanics worth mastering all while working on most computers.  If you don't already own this game it should be your priority to make a purchase for this product as soon as possible.  You will not regret it.

First off to start this review I'd like to say that this game is a must have on steam, It's been on numerous sales and has one of the best and most weird communities. I have gladly dumped over 500 hours in this game and about 200 in the other games, I had another account on steam but I lost it's password, therefore I happily repurchased the Mount&Blade Collection.
To summarize this game in a few words this game would be : Death, Medieval Times, humongous battles ranging from 2 to 200 men, if you use mods it can reach to 500 men battles, Different Culture Castles, Sieges, Best Combat System and Amusing Horse Deaths.
Alright, now that I've sed all that You can probably picture what Epicness awaits you after you purchase this masterpiece!
As you start the game you get the Generic RPG choise, a man or a woman, but chose wisely because the Mount&Blade world takes place in a sexist environment, If you choose to be a female character, if you decide to become a vassal of a king you will not be awarded the Fief you would receive if you were a man, and the Lords treat you like a fragile being when you meet them before Battle and can sometimes insult you! You can take part in feasts, tournaments, votations, marriages, Duels for a lady's honour among other things, My favourite Hobby is to Run down peasants with my knights.
As your men gain experience you get to level them up to more powerful medieval forces, From A peasant with a stick to an Epic Knight, there are several factions with lots of different units each faction has they're weaknesses and strengths. You get to Destroy and burn villages to the ground and capture castles and Cities if you are mighty enough.

FOR MOUNT AND BLADE NAPOLEONIC WARS (I might edit in a Warband vanilla review later):
Spawned in a room with my horse, couldn't move anywhere. People were fighting outside; I had to go help my teammates.
Hopped off my horse, ran into the kitchen. Turned around to see my friend slaughter my dismounted horse.
After expressing my sorrow through chat text the teammate simply replied with "he was a deserter" then went downstairs and started ♥♥♥♥ing playing on the piano.
Suddenly the glass window broke behind him and as he slumped to the ground I ran outside to see our base being overrun. I was killed quickly.
As I respawned as a cavalry unit (in the open this time) I saw another horse in the distance and the rider was killing my friends.
I followed him and eventually made him chase me through an open field away from the massacre in the suburbs.
I got one hit on him but he eventually turned around and in what seemed to be a temporary jousting match he stabbed my horse with his sword and I fell to the ground.
He started circling me for about half a minute, like a hunter and its prey.
I kept swiping him away with my sword, and eventually he rode away then hopped off his horse.
He turned slowly towards me and started walking towards me pulling his sword out.
After about a three minute chase the final showdown had begun.
It was here when I killed him, a quick sideswipe to his throat.
And as I praised his fighting skills in the chat below, I see words from this brave soldier I had so recently killed.
"Nah that was ♥♥♥♥in ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, ♥♥♥♥ you man."
Mount and Blade Napoleonic Wars: 10/10

A game that I liked from the start. Once I started playing this I felt like I was actually in a real apocalypse. This game really teaches me to conserve my ammo (I can't stress enough how many times I've died because I used up all the ammo). Over time, I got scared of playing single player, so I tried multiplayer. Let me tell you, it is so fun playing with other people. There are different maps with different game modes. The game mode I like best is PvP since I can easily kill other survivors without feeling guilty. The best part about the game is the atmosphere it provides. You'll feel intimidated at times, you'll feel crazy when you play alone, and most of the time you'll just feel like giving up. I wouldn't say the game itself is scary, but it does have some horror aspects put in it. If you want a good ol' fashioned zombie outbreak game with realistic features, buy Contagion. The price is worth it. $15 for an awesome game? I wouldn't even hesitate to buying it.

Firstly, I want to say that the games I've gotten into that were balanced were hella fun.
That said, it seems to be a pay-to-win kind of game. The fact, for instance, that you're only given one kit (character) slot per faction unless you pay for the second slot, is kind of dumb. I enjoy sniping, but occasionally you need to have something more mid/close-range to be of any use in a battle. Can't do that in this game.Takes a little bit to unlock bolt-action rifles (really not so bad), but you can't upgrade them to scoped - only change iron sights. To get a scoped BA, you instead have to either pay for boosts or grind weeks (probably months if you're like me and play 2-3 games a day) to get the scoped version of the sniper... And, to qualify that, a BA with iron sights is pretty much useless against an enemy with scoped BAs.
Game-to-game balancing of teams is also woeful. I've been in more games than I can remember where we lost solely because the other team had like 3-4 Tigers and we had no armor and no air. I also spent an entire day being 2-4 players short as US. We would be 4v6'ing and another German player would connect...
Could be so much more fun, but the pay-to-win/ridiculous grindfest that it appears to be combined with the horrible team balancing led me to far more frustrating games than fun ones. This really wouldn't bother me, but the fact they sit there and claim "We wish to create a healthy, solid and well-balanced game and community, where you can get a great experience playing the game, no matter how much money you spend!" is...well, a lie. You can't give such huge bonuses to spending money and claim to be looking to foster balance regardless of how much money you're spending.

Simply put: I liked Call Of Duty Ghosts.
Still with me? Screaming "You're just a damn CoD fanboy"? Well there's nothing I can do, since you're on the other side of the screen. But yes, I do like Ghosts. I've had a pretty rocky history with CoD. I started playing with Modern Warfare, and I loved it. It still remains in my heart as one of the best online shooters ever. I feel like things took another road with Modern Warfare 3. I liked the story, but everything else... you know what I mean. I played all the way through the series ending with Black ops 2, and I felt done with CoD. But as many others did, they bought Ghosts for the hell of it. And while others see Ghosts as bringing the beloved series to a downfall, I think the changes were for the best.
I played this originally on PC, and later on Xbox One. Both systems had the same quality game, but PC had... problems. The game had an awful launch. The lack of dedicated servers, horrible optimization, and changes no one liked, it was destined to be doomed. While all of those things should've been ready on day one (and they weren't), it's fixed now. I can run the game like a champ, and it's great on performance. Still with the lack of dedicated servers though, it's a small issue.
I enjoyed the campaign. I don't really need to get into that. It was original, and it was fresh.
The online multiplayer is where we all resort to though in the end. Putting it frank, it works. The PC version is probably the worst as far as the community goes though. Only 4-6 thousand people online on a good night (46k players on a slow Monday morning on XB1) makes this horrible to find matches. I'm sure even the Wii U has more dedicated players. Just throwing this out there too, don't buy any DLC, because you'll be lucky to find any matches with that DLC. But once you can get into a match, things are usually okay, if hackers aren't present. But one of my favorite things is also something everyone hates: the large maps. I've been playing the Battlefield series for years, and I love the vast size of those maps. While Ghosts maps aren't nearly as big, they're big enough to have good spawn spots and such. Sure, camping isn't the greatest thing ever, but sometimes you just need to overcome them and be a good team player. At least, I was able to, in my 30+ hours into the online alone. I think customization is great too. While character creators aren't really needed in a game like this, it's a fresh spin for newcomers. The guns feel great, and sound amazing.
Then, you have some other modes that, unfortunately you won't be able to touch on the PC version due to the lack of players. The "Squads" mode sounded truly unique. You can create a squad, and have those AI players go into other people’s games, and try to beat them. You would train each AI character in the regular online mode, and when you felt they were ready, you'd send them into Squads. As I mentioned though, this cool RPG like mode isn't usable, because no one uses it. Extinction mode is also a very fresh new mode. Like Zombies from WaW, Blops and Blops 2, you'll be fending off against aliens trying to invade Earth. Sound generic? It's really not. You'll make your own custom loadouts, and it's crucial to play with other players, because it's it gets pretty hectic. It also consists of its own campaign, and it continues through the DLC packs. Again though, no one plays this mode, so it's sort of a lost cause. If you play on Xbox or Playstation though, I doubt you won't be able to have a good time.
So in short, the PC version did (and still) has problems. But with some of the best gunplay around, Ghosts is a fantastic entry to the Call of Duty franchise.

An amazing atmospheric zombie adventure!  The story isn't overly dramatic, but does suffer from the survivor syndrome storyline that we typically see in modern zombie productions.  Don't let that sway you away.  This zombie plat-former doesn't disappoint.  The artistic direction was spot on in this game.  When I close my eyes at night Deadlight is exactly how I imagine the zombie apocalypse to look like.  General degradation of the city and buildings, decaying bodies (both dead and alive), the environment saturated in filth and gore and chaotic collateral damage from the post-apocalyptic zombie aftermath all set the mood for this intriguing story.  Game play was easy.  There were only two to three challenging parts, however, this didn't take away from the overall experience.  It's a relief game.  Something to play between your most played games for a break.  Seeing how this was a console port I was pretty concerned, however, controls, for the most part were not a major issue.  You are limited to predefined set of keys and that is it.  Minor bug issues arose, but nothing that affected the game play or takes away from the overall experience.  Pick this up on sale and enjoy!

Deadlight oozes a lot potential and promise during the first 60-90 minutes, but unfortunately it fails to live up to that potential the rest of the way. The game is divided into three acts: The first act plays like a high-quality survival-horror platformer with limited focus on combat. The atmosphere is terrific and this is by far the high point of the campaign. The second act, though, stumbles horribly into a platforming/puzzle-solving mess that's made annoying by the game's awful controls that just never feel right at all. The third act strives to get back to the style of the first act, and at times succeeds in doing so, but unfortunately it's just not able to recapture that early magic.
From a visual standpoint, Deadlight is simply stunning. It has a really great art style that will make you stop and admire the gloomy Pacific Northwest backdrop. The game also features some top-notch sound design. From a story standpoint, it's mostly a forgettable tale that's riddled with bad voicework.
Deadlight feels like a game that really could've been something special if the devs had stuck to the formula of the first act, tightened the controls, and made the puzzles more challenging than they were. Instead it's a game that begins to fall apart after the first 90 minutes before picking itself up during the final stretch and crossing the finish line with a limp. Decent yet disappointing.

This game is so good but does have one or two flaws. It's an open world shooter experience set on a tropical island that allows you to role play in some ways. After being captured by pirates you're forced to become a bad♥♥♥♥♥survivalist to save your friends from being sold into slavery. The setup is beautifully done with great characters, environment and lighting with mature content and funny dialogue. Getting around the island is made immersive by the games superbly crafted animations. The ending even gives you a big choice which leads to one of two endings. The flaws include limited graphical finesse on certain objects and NPC character models. Also the save game options are a bit broken. A second play through is usually bugged as you have to overwrite an old save to start over and it's nigh on impossible to delete the previous save to start over from scratch, at least for me. The multiplayer is surprisingly fleshed out for a first person shooter and can offer an additional 10 to 20 hours of game play on top of the 50 hours I clocked on the main campaign. As a final verdict I give Farcry 3 a superb 8/10.

I've heard this game getting some negative attention, but having gotten to Act 3, I can tell you it is fairly well undeserved. There are a couple minor control issues, mostly centered around climbing quickly while being chased by helicopters, lol, but outside of that, the game controls are fairly seamless. The game itself is fun as hell. It's a 2-D scroller with a 3-D background which looks really cool in a sort of Apocalyptic Noire fashion. The gameplay itself is fun. You get weapons sparingly and always need to make decision regarding how you are going to deal with the zombies (or Shadows as they are called in this game). You have a stamina bar which is drained when running or engaging in melee combat. You have a very limited amount of bullets for any guns you find. You are however quite acrobatic, and running, jumping, diving, and rolling are equally important from a tactical standpoint. There are also som cool trap sequences, and in many parts, you can use the environment to your advantage as well.
Finally, the story is also really quite interesting, and unlike most games, the "secrets" (aka hidden objects) are very easy to find, although with the undead on your tail, you may not have time to grab them, lol
I think this is a definite must own. It really is a very good game in my opinion.

Battles are fun, everything else is badly implemented. I have run into graphics glitches that cause my character to become headless and maps to become black and invisible. There is also a memory leak problem; the longer you play the game, the choppier the frame rates become. This isn't a problem affecting everyone though. Likewise the graphics glitches I mentioned also doesn't affect everyone.
Things that are fun:
1. Battles
Things that are not fun:
1. Chasing cattles
2. Chasing bandits
3. Chasing ladies
4. Chasing lords
5. Chasing spies
Boy that's a lot of chasing.
Chasing cattles, more specifically, herding them, is not a needed game mechanic. In fact, there is no reason to have cattles in the game at all; it doesn't add anything good to the game. Cattle mechanic can easily be replaced by something more fun. Chasing bandits, where the bandits are faster than you, takes forever. You have to actually corner them on the map to do these quests. The next is looking for bandit hide outs, which is equally boring. You need to be right next to a bandit hideout for it to appear on the  map. You need to chase ladies and lords around for quests. You want to hand in and get quests from the ladies and lords, but the ladies and lords aren't always at the same faction or the same castle. So you actually have to ask other lords in their faction to find where they are. Sometimes they disappear and you can never find them, so that means the quest is an auto-fail. Chasing spies is another ridiculous quest. If you don't know how to chase spies, you will auto-fail the quest. To even complete the quest, you need decent tracking skill, which the game doesn't tell you.
The whole chasing problem is worsened by real time travelling. I wish they could abstract the over-map travelling, because there doesn't seem to be too many positive reason for the player to have to move across the map in real time. I actually don't hate moving around in real time, I just hate the combination of real time movement and chasing quests.
The next point is the lack of tutorial in the game. The only tutorial the game offers is for combat and nothing else. Everything else in the game you have to look it up on the wiki, the game forum, or learn trial by error.
The only good thing the game has going for it is the combat. If the developer improves non-combat aspects of the game, such as better quests and political interactions, this could be the best game I have ever played, but no such luck.
And yes, I still recommend this game just for the battle.

This game is so good but does have one or two flaws. It's an open world shooter experience set on a tropical island that allows you to role play in some ways. After being captured by pirates you're forced to become a bad♥♥♥♥♥survivalist to save your friends from being sold into slavery. The setup is beautifully done with great characters, environment and lighting with mature content and funny dialogue. Getting around the island is made immersive by the games superbly crafted animations. The ending even gives you a big choice which leads to one of two endings. The flaws include limited graphical finesse on certain objects and NPC character models. Also the save game options are a bit broken. A second play through is usually bugged as you have to overwrite an old save to start over and it's nigh on impossible to delete the previous save to start over from scratch, at least for me. The multiplayer is surprisingly fleshed out for a first person shooter and can offer an additional 10 to 20 hours of game play on top of the 50 hours I clocked on the main campaign. As a final verdict I give Farcry 3 a superb 8/10.

Deadlight and Limbo are pretty similar game, except the former excels at doing many things than the latter. Graphic wise, it's a decent one. I, for one, won't complain about the visual. It's pretty sharp and background is detailed enough. However like Limbo, you can't see the protagonist well because most of the times he's just a silhouette. Kind of weird, but just minor annoyance.
As a platformer, this is what you usually see from platformer game. You run from enemies, jump around, manipulate items to proceed further into the game.
Control. This is platformer, so it'd be best if you whip out your gamepad to play. This game, being a Microsoft product, supports XBOX 360 out of the box. Older Dinput controllers can just plug x360ce and the game will recognize your gamepad instantly. The layout is pretty neat and friendly for fingers, but aiming can be awkward since it uses right thumb stick and could be a problem during quick event where you need to kill your enemies for example.
Sound, frankly I don't pay attention much. There's enough tension to keep my attention to my character and his surroundings.
Levels are static, so don't expect replayability much. Once you finish the game I think there's not much you can do. Except... achievements perhaps? Level design is pretty great though, and certainly for platformer it's the main aspect. You're not forced to backtrack much when progressing and most of the times level presentation is clear enough so you don't get lost on what to do.
Verdict: Great game and can entertain you for hours. When it's on sale you would do well to get the game.

As of May 2014, after a couple of patches and two DLC map packs, Ghosts has finally matured into a playable CoD title more or less worthy of the franchise.
Although the matchmaking is far from ideal and the player base has suffered because the poor initial port, I can finally stop hating Ghosts with a passion, look at it as a reasonable CoD game and have fun with it.
Compared to Black Ops 2 it still needs a powerful system to run smoothly, IMHO too much power because of poor optimization, but at least it has improved to the point where it can run almost as smoothly as Black Ops 2 - although the latter is superior in most ways that count in a fast shooter.

Battles are fun, everything else is badly implemented. I have run into graphics glitches that cause my character to become headless and maps to become black and invisible. There is also a memory leak problem; the longer you play the game, the choppier the frame rates become. This isn't a problem affecting everyone though. Likewise the graphics glitches I mentioned also doesn't affect everyone.
Things that are fun:
1. Battles
Things that are not fun:
1. Chasing cattles
2. Chasing bandits
3. Chasing ladies
4. Chasing lords
5. Chasing spies
Boy that's a lot of chasing.
Chasing cattles, more specifically, herding them, is not a needed game mechanic. In fact, there is no reason to have cattles in the game at all; it doesn't add anything good to the game. Cattle mechanic can easily be replaced by something more fun. Chasing bandits, where the bandits are faster than you, takes forever. You have to actually corner them on the map to do these quests. The next is looking for bandit hide outs, which is equally boring. You need to be right next to a bandit hideout for it to appear on the  map. You need to chase ladies and lords around for quests. You want to hand in and get quests from the ladies and lords, but the ladies and lords aren't always at the same faction or the same castle. So you actually have to ask other lords in their faction to find where they are. Sometimes they disappear and you can never find them, so that means the quest is an auto-fail. Chasing spies is another ridiculous quest. If you don't know how to chase spies, you will auto-fail the quest. To even complete the quest, you need decent tracking skill, which the game doesn't tell you.
The whole chasing problem is worsened by real time travelling. I wish they could abstract the over-map travelling, because there doesn't seem to be too many positive reason for the player to have to move across the map in real time. I actually don't hate moving around in real time, I just hate the combination of real time movement and chasing quests.
The next point is the lack of tutorial in the game. The only tutorial the game offers is for combat and nothing else. Everything else in the game you have to look it up on the wiki, the game forum, or learn trial by error.
The only good thing the game has going for it is the combat. If the developer improves non-combat aspects of the game, such as better quests and political interactions, this could be the best game I have ever played, but no such luck.
And yes, I still recommend this game just for the battle.

Imagine the original, sidescrolling Prince of Persia set in the gloomy Pacific Northwest. During a zombie apocalypse. In 1986. With awesome 3D graphics. Times ten.  Baby, you got a stew going.
It really is an amazing game. Unfortunately, there were some pretty big cons:
1. There was no sound in the cutscenes.  From reading on the internet it's apparently a pretty widespread problem that's being completely ignored by the developers.  There are some hacky fixes like copying over a certain dll from another game (didn't work for me), and alt-tabbing in and out of the game during the cutscenes to restore the sound (worked about 90% of the time for me).  The going theory is this is another symptom of ♥♥♥♥♥♥-console-port-itis. I didn't have any other "technical" issues other than this.
2. There were 2 or 3 absolutely unforgivingly hard points in the game where I died 9 trillion times on the same "jump" or "fight" and had to watch the death screen, fade to black, pop back to the last checkpoint, then listen to triggered monologue again. And again. And again. Really annoying. I remember reading that the developers of Super Meat Boy spent a large chunk of time making dying in that game not discouraging to the player because it happens a lot.  This game could have benefitted from a little of that.
3. Pretty short, probably about 4-6 hours long, depending on playstyle and achievement hunting. You probably won't get all of them on your first play through, and winning does unlock a nightmare mode, so who knows.

Deadlight is a very atmospheric experience: its plot serves to tell a simple, yet powerful tale; its visuals are an effective mix of 3D graphics and a 2D sidescroller perspective; the game plays with its colour palette and lighting; the gameplay is a mix of platforming and survival horror elements – combat really is the last resort here. The puzzles aren't very complex or challenging, but they are thought-provoking enough to keep the experience engaging.
Many of Deadlight's greatest features are due to the appropriately gauged ambition of its designers. The development team knew that they could not make everything work with a low budget and so few hands on the project. For that reason they stuck only with things that worked for the game. What you're left with is a short, sweet, highly atmospheric and engrossing indie platformer.
The setting is very unoriginal and the controls sometimes seem a bit awkward when using a mouse and keyboard, but every aspect of the game reinforces its creepy atmosphere – and this is why Deadlight succeeds. Grab it in a sale though, because the 4 hours it takes to complete the game are not much for £10 – even with the unlockable extras that the game has to offer.

Contagion is an amazing Co-op Survival game that can be highly addictive (in my case). Contagion features Five impressive game modes,, each including it's own styles of gameplay:
+Escape
+Extraction
+Hunted
+Classic (x2)
+Flatline(DLC Bundle/not yet released)
* Escape puts you and other players into the world with an Objective- Escape the undead. It is recommended that you raise the difficulty (if easy/normal) if playing with 3+ players.
* Extraction again teams up the players against the dead to rescue survivors around the map. This mode can be difficult. (play hard with 5-6 Players)
* Hunted pits Players against eachother - but the undead still wonder the streets? thats right! watch your back because once you begin shooting at other players, the Undead will come for you. no recommended difficulty.
*As well as the main modes, Contagion has two Classic modes that are very similar to ZPS. Both are player only modes and support larger servers. The first Classic mode is very similar to Escape but with only players. The other is a timed survival themed mode.
* Flatline SHOULD be a wave based survival.
This game plays well on low preformance PCs, however it greatly reduces the graphics to a simple toonish feel.
If playing Solo, i Recommend playing Escape or Extraction, Just set the Difficulty to its highest setting.

Let me start by saying I really enjoyed my time spent playing, even though I think the story was a bit lackluster. The gameplay and environment were both very enjoyable, enough so that I spent nearly 30 hours playing and may still keep playing just to complete what I didn't finish earlier. There is a huge open world to explore and plenty to do besides the main story, including multiplayer and co-op modes. I warn you that while the endgame was disappointing, the overall gameplay was worth it to me.

(For tl;dr people skip to the end)
Even though this isn't the new and shiny Far Cry 4 or Primal, I can Guarentee you will get your money's worth. Here are some of the reasons this is a must play for any FPS fanatic or really any gamer, who appreciates a well crafted action packed adventure.
1. It is one of the only FPS games with actual charcters, a problem even Far Cry 4 struggles with. Not only is Vaas a very hateable villain, but Jason actually has a character arc, going from a whiney rich inner city white guy, to a vicious, psychotic murderer pumped up with more drugs than Micheal Jackson. Jason also has a real reason to fight against Vaas' Pirates, being that Vaas captured his friends, unlike in FC4, where the only motif of fighting for a resistance you don't know, in country you've never been to, from a ruler you don't know or are surpressed by only because your mom wanted you to dumb her ashes in the Himalaya. Maybe it's just me but if I found out there was a civil war in the country I was in I would leave ASAP.
2. The Island feels so real and natural; the animals are well animated, the locals are cool, the villains are intimidating, and the weapons are, as in every FC game, amazing.
3. It's 10-20 dollars cheaper than FC4 and FCP respectively
4. It's so fun and hooking, the missions never feel too long, the combat is smooth, the cutscenes are beautiful and lenghty, without being annoying, and most importantly it's 10 times better than FC2 in every way.
(tl;dr) 1. best story/character development
2. realistic atmosphere
3. cheaper than FC4/FCP
4. hooking; well designed

What, then, makes it so hard?  Their numbers.  That's typical of any zombie game, but when you have a handful of bullets, and zombies that only die when you hit them in the head (as it should be), then man, does that make for a difficult game.  All that being said, I'm hooked.  Someone finally got the genre right, in my books.
Grab this game, by all means.  I could use the backup.

This game doesn't quite come together.
The best thing I can say is that the theme song is beautiful.
Some of the sets are visually impressive, but the story is rather underwhelming, the dialog is unnatural, the voice acting is bad, and there is a segment in the middle ("The Rat") that doesn't quite mesh with the setting and strains suspension of disbelief to the breaking point. The first third of the game is ridiculously easy even after the part where they teach you the controls, and after that, the challenge is more in the controls than it solving puzzles. Indeed, many of the scenes aren't something you can think through in advance; it's try-and-error. This is made more frustrating by the fact that when the premise isn't, "What would make sense here?", but "What moves does the game want from me this time?", the environment should at least behave exactly the same each time -- which of course doesn't seem to be the case. It also doesn't help that the backstory comes as a 60 page diary, so your choices are starting your new game without knowing your character's personal backstory, or reading 60 pages of badly written diary entries. At least of course, they are small pages with not a lot of text on them, and some are missing -- oh yeah, didn't I mention that? Some of the pages are missing, and you'll find them as you traverse places you've never been before. Um, yeah.
The studio also talked up the fact that the game is set in the '80s (See what they did there? Two things with a following, '80s, and zombies, it must have seemed like a sure hit and/or license to print money.), but in the game, that makes practically no difference at all. Your load animation is a tape deck, there are three vintage video games you can find, and "commies" are mentioned, that's about it, and none of it makes a difference. Sure, the studio are right when pointing out that there are "no cell phones, no computers", but six month into a zombocalypse, I wouldn't expect to get much mileage out of either, anyway, so that doesn't have much of an impact. Heck, even if  computers were common and worked, I wouldn't expect deranged mountain man Randy to bother with them.
On balance, Limbo, a game that doesn't even attempt to do include many of these things (voice acting, anything worth being called a story, etc.) ends up being the better game for it -- of course, having a spectacular, distinct look and somewhat better controls helps, too.

Deadlight is a mix of a platformer, horror and action game. This somewhat unique cocktail works surprisingly well and offers a very enjoyable experience from start to finish. Lack of originality aside, Deadlight may appear to be yet another game placed in a zombie apocalypse setting, but it barely falls for the traps these games often set.
As a platformer it does pretty much everything right. The puzzles are fun and never frustrating. The design is incredibly well done, often adding another decimal to its 2D appearance. As an action game its on the same path: The combat is quite exciting, where you have to make the right choice every time. Whether you head in with an axe or a gun, taking on too many mobs will likely result in death. Once you finally get a gun the game doesn't exactly become any easier as the ammo is scarce.
The story is rich and enticing. By gathering the collectables such as diary pages you slowly start to understand the story and its characters better, offering a lot of added depth.
Because of the nearly flawless checkpoint system you won't really be angered by the occasional death that is caused by the somewhat poorly responsive controls. The visuals are one of the best I've ever seen in a 2D world, but there were some flickering and flashing issues in outside areas.
The small problems aside, Deadlight is one of the best platformers released in the past couple of years, reminding me of gems from the SNES. Anyone who's looking for a blast from the past should look no further.

Review date - Jan12th, 2014.
Game still in 'Beta' stage at time of review.
Okay. Contagion is something else! You think you know zombie games? You've played a bit of Left 4 Dead, Dead Island, Nazi Zombie Army, or other games? Forget everything you know.
Ammo is SCARCE.
Zombies will ONLY die from head trauma (bullet or melee)
If a teammate goes down - you CANNOT help them up.
Medkits or other healing methods are EXTREMELY RARE.
These are not negatives though, don't get me wrong. This is straight up a tactical co-op zombie FPS.
For one, each level has a certain degree of randomness. Not just zombies and weapon drops, but mission items (such as keys), and barricared doors will be randomly spawned to create unique pathing and situational approaches depending on the new level design.
Your aim matters - and so does ammo management! Contagion has the unique feature of being able to not only drop a weapon for team mates, but also to empty the weapon of ammo first, or just drop unused ammo for weapons you're not carrying. This promotes a great deal of discussion as you find your squad boxxed into a corner, knowing the horde of zombies is bearing down, and quickly sharing ammo so everyone can survive.
My only complaints really at this time of writing are cosmetic ones - some items in the game world will move and can be knocked about, half-life style, but others can't. And the zombie hordes can look quite "samey" after a while, with a relatively small pool of character skins chosen from. Some enhanced physics interaction and randomised skin elements (pants, tops, damage, blood, dirt, etc) on the zombies would add a lot to the immersion.
TL;DR If you're even a little bit into Left 4 Dead but would like something less arcadey, and more focused on the creepy horror atmosphere and survival aspect, GET THIS GAME :)

So, I'm not the best person to make review... But here goes:
When I looked at this game, I wasn't expecting that much. My brother suggested that I'd buy this game.

Gameplay:
I haven't played a game like this before, but it was pretty much everything I wanted. You begin as character you make yourself. You decide origin (ex. Noble birth, the son of a warrior), childhood training/experience, occupation before the game, and your reason for setting out, all of these affecting the different stats and items you begin with. After the character creation, you have to go through a short series of quests (which I believe are skipable), in which after you decide what you want to do. Want to wander around fighting enemy armies and bandits with your army? Become a vassal to a king? Want to own a town? How about several towns? A whole kingdom? It's all possible in this game.
The battles are in 3rd person, where you control your character and can give orders to your soldiers if you want.
Graphics:
The graphics aren't top notch, but they are still pretty good and needed for this game, as it would lag too much otherwise. The game is in 3D, with 3D graphics. (Wow, this was a bit short. Oh well, let's move on.)
Music:
The music is nothing extraordinary, but it fits well and doesn't distract you.
Bugs/Issues:
I have encountered two issues that are somewhat annoying, but doesn't make the game unplayable. The first thing being occational graphic glitches, where the graphics ♥♥♥♥ up. Alt+tab should work, however... Doing that could mean that the game won't let you return, forcing you to turn off the game through the task killer. My fix for that is running windowed, and pressing alt+enter to get fullscreen. And then whenever you want to switch, just press alt+enter and there should be no problems.

Let's get all of the bad out first, shall we? The game looks incredibly dated, shiny armor and helmets aside. It's technically unimpressive, though you can get mods to make it more so. Some of the controls can be rather clunky, and while there is a tutorial, it leaves out several things that could be better explained. Not to mention, you could go a fairly long time without finding out you could control your army with the number keys and the F buttons. But these are minor complaints that can be solved with some research.
That all said, Mount and Blade: Warband is an incredible game, and it gives you the reigns to see how Calradia forms. Join factions, betray said factions and join another, help a claimant claim their throne, or just say '♥♥♥♥ it' and make your own faction! Want an army that numbers in the hundreds? Sure. Want to take on whole armies by yourself? Have fun! Want to only use lances and joust armies down, or do nothing but shoot arrows into people's skulls? Go for it, kid.
The amount of control that this game gives you is impressive, to say the least. It even lets you customize how difficult you want the game to be. How much damage you or your army takes, enemy AI strength, teammate AI, and the number of troops on the field at a time can all be customizeable, to make a difficulty you feel comfortable with.

Battles are fun, everything else is badly implemented. I have run into graphics glitches that cause my character to become headless and maps to become black and invisible. There is also a memory leak problem; the longer you play the game, the choppier the frame rates become. This isn't a problem affecting everyone though. Likewise the graphics glitches I mentioned also doesn't affect everyone.
Things that are fun:
1. Battles
Things that are not fun:
1. Chasing cattles
2. Chasing bandits
3. Chasing ladies
4. Chasing lords
5. Chasing spies
Boy that's a lot of chasing.
Chasing cattles, more specifically, herding them, is not a needed game mechanic. In fact, there is no reason to have cattles in the game at all; it doesn't add anything good to the game. Cattle mechanic can easily be replaced by something more fun. Chasing bandits, where the bandits are faster than you, takes forever. You have to actually corner them on the map to do these quests. The next is looking for bandit hide outs, which is equally boring. You need to be right next to a bandit hideout for it to appear on the  map. You need to chase ladies and lords around for quests. You want to hand in and get quests from the ladies and lords, but the ladies and lords aren't always at the same faction or the same castle. So you actually have to ask other lords in their faction to find where they are. Sometimes they disappear and you can never find them, so that means the quest is an auto-fail. Chasing spies is another ridiculous quest. If you don't know how to chase spies, you will auto-fail the quest. To even complete the quest, you need decent tracking skill, which the game doesn't tell you.
The whole chasing problem is worsened by real time travelling. I wish they could abstract the over-map travelling, because there doesn't seem to be too many positive reason for the player to have to move across the map in real time. I actually don't hate moving around in real time, I just hate the combination of real time movement and chasing quests.
The next point is the lack of tutorial in the game. The only tutorial the game offers is for combat and nothing else. Everything else in the game you have to look it up on the wiki, the game forum, or learn trial by error.
The only good thing the game has going for it is the combat. If the developer improves non-combat aspects of the game, such as better quests and political interactions, this could be the best game I have ever played, but no such luck.
And yes, I still recommend this game just for the battle.

Alright, this is another survival horror FPS, the spiritual successor to Zombie Panic Source is now available via Early Access. I want to start off by saying that this game looks visually appealing. It is beautiful. There are only a few maps available at the moment, as it is in beta, but you do get a few different game modes out of it. You can escort AI-controlled survivors, battle zombies as a human or battle humans as a zombie, or my personal favorite, escape from the police department in an objective-based co-op experience. There are a lot of great ideas, and the price tag does indeed turn some people away from this game when the alternative is Free to Play. Both games are technically in beta and both will only get better in time. Contagion is a very fun experience and worth the money. It is an entirely different game than No More Room In Hell and they can't truly be compared with each other because they are trying to achieve different goals. When you die to the zombies in Contagion, your corpse will rise and you will walk among the dead. You will control your own zombie with the intention to do harm to your former allies. The levels are large, and the zombies are plentiful. You can host your own games or play on dedicated servers. If you are looking for one more push before you buy this, I strongly recommend that you check out YouTube for that last push.

Deadlight, a fun action/shooter/survival horror/puzzle/platformer.  Music and atmosphere were beautifully done.  After I played just a little bit of it I realized right away why they also offered a package deal with the game AND the official soundtrack.  It's a bold attempt to meld all 5 of the genre's I mentioned above into one game but lets take an honest look at each element they tried to include.  Action (as in combat) was awkward and sticky but after you get your first gun it kinda goes away.  Shooting was fun and fulfilling although they never let you have a gun when you could really use one and vice versa.  It definitely is survival horror because I have never seen a smaller quantity of zombies equaling death ratio before, if only 2 zombies close the distance and grapple you then you may as well reload a save right then because they can combo you from full health to dead without you getting any chance of running or fighting; it intensifies the experience but it's annoying as hell.  Puzzles are barely more complicated than move box to high ledge so you can grab high ledge.  The platforming may be the most fluid part of the game and it's very fun watching this grizzley middle-aged bearded man parkour his way across rooftop after rooftop.
Cheap and fun, just the way I like my indie games.  A couple things could have been tweaked here and there but nobody's perfect.  What Deadlight does do it does well and I'll be playing it again soon looking for all the hidden items.

So, I'm not the best person to make review... But here goes:
When I looked at this game, I wasn't expecting that much. My brother suggested that I'd buy this game.
After 2-3 hours, this game had already become extremely addictive.
Gameplay:
I haven't played a game like this before, but it was pretty much everything I wanted. You begin as character you make yourself. You decide origin (ex. Noble birth, the son of a warrior), childhood training/experience, occupation before the game, and your reason for setting out, all of these affecting the different stats and items you begin with. After the character creation, you have to go through a short series of quests (which I believe are skipable), in which after you decide what you want to do. Want to wander around fighting enemy armies and bandits with your army? Become a vassal to a king? Want to own a town? How about several towns? A whole kingdom? It's all possible in this game.
The battles are in 3rd person, where you control your character and can give orders to your soldiers if you want.
Graphics:
The graphics aren't top notch, but they are still pretty good and needed for this game, as it would lag too much otherwise. The game is in 3D, with 3D graphics. (Wow, this was a bit short. Oh well, let's move on.)
Music:
The music is nothing extraordinary, but it fits well and doesn't distract you.
Bugs/Issues:
I have encountered two issues that are somewhat annoying, but doesn't make the game unplayable. The first thing being occational graphic glitches, where the graphics ♥♥♥♥ up. Alt+tab should work, however... Doing that could mean that the game won't let you return, forcing you to turn off the game through the task killer. My fix for that is running windowed, and pressing alt+enter to get fullscreen. And then whenever you want to switch, just press alt+enter and there should be no problems.

Let's get all of the bad out first, shall we? The game looks incredibly dated, shiny armor and helmets aside. It's technically unimpressive, though you can get mods to make it more so. Some of the controls can be rather clunky, and while there is a tutorial, it leaves out several things that could be better explained. Not to mention, you could go a fairly long time without finding out you could control your army with the number keys and the F buttons. But these are minor complaints that can be solved with some research.
That all said, Mount and Blade: Warband is an incredible game, and it gives you the reigns to see how Calradia forms. Join factions, betray said factions and join another, help a claimant claim their throne, or just say '♥♥♥♥ it' and make your own faction! Want an army that numbers in the hundreds? Sure. Want to take on whole armies by yourself? Have fun! Want to only use lances and joust armies down, or do nothing but shoot arrows into people's skulls? Go for it, kid.
The amount of control that this game gives you is impressive, to say the least. It even lets you customize how difficult you want the game to be. How much damage you or your army takes, enemy AI strength, teammate AI, and the number of troops on the field at a time can all be customizeable, to make a difficulty you feel comfortable with.
Mount and Blade: Warband is a refreshing game in which you get to rule your men and your country however you deem fit, and in an era where games get increasingly narrow and never let go of your hand. It'll beat your life to a pulp, and sell the rest of it to a ransom broker for some quick denars, and it's worth every penny.

I must say that too many people ♥♥♥♥♥ and moan about this so called "pay-2-win" game. Yes, like almost EVERY OTHER MMO out there, grinding can be avoided with a simple in-game transaction. However, just because you buy the higher-tier gear, that does not mean you will play better. This game is based on skill, teamwork, and patience, not wallet size. I have followed this game from before the steam launch and the yogscast fiasco, and it has come a long way. Yes, my hours on steam are quite low but I logged at least 150+ hours on the browser based version. A dedicated team and a growing fan-base have helped this game glow. Yes, some features are currently lacking, but this is also an early-access game, so keep in mind you are playing a BETA, a beta that is FAR from its finished product. With great, content filled updates and a large list of things the developers hope to add, from 64 v 64 battles, new maps ranging from small skirmishes to massive regions, and  new factions, fronts, and weapons of war, this game could become the crown jewel of the WWII FPS world. I urge you to give the game and the developers a chance before turning your nose to a so-called "buggy, expensive piece of trash". Yes, there are bugs and yes there are hackers, but all will hopefully fixed in due time.

PROS:

-It pays to spray in close quarters
-Each team has their "go to" overpowered weapon

CONS:

-The occasional hacker

This is not your regular zombie survival game you know from each corner of the internet. This is something different, this feels more important, more realistic. This is way better than anything else you might encounter.
You really feel the need to survive, to find your friends and family and to save them.
There is no slashing, shooting and explosions to kill your way to the end. I thought so in the beginning, but you'll notice very quickly that you can do this as much as you want, to no avail in the end.
Just. Run. Away! Kill only these who give you no other choice, but then run again! You can't fight them all! Try it, I'll promise you, you'll fail.
The controls feel just a bit clunky, which is most of the time no problem, but you might die because you accidently jumped into the wrong direction a few times.
But the real reason I write this review, is the story.
I am amazed! Your character (Randall) feels like a stranger in the beginning. Just an old man who wants to survive. Instead he has an interesting backstory to develop, something he can't remember by himself right now, but his memories will return. While that happens, maybe you can try to identify yourself with him. You feel the importance of his actions, as much as you'll losing hope for this world. He does just as well.
The scenery feels realistic and convincing, as much as the scenario in the background. The world is going to end, that's the message you can't avoid to understand. And while that happens, people are going to get crazy.
The more you progress in game, the more you find the helplessness of the world. Hope just fades away.
But there is something else nobody tried before..
This is not the year 2025, nothing what "might be happen in the future".
This game feels like a novel to me, an action-thriller of the good ones, because the date we are talking about is 1986, in Seattle.
While this may seem unimportant to many people playing this game, let me light a candle for you.
If it would be 2025, some people might "go crazy" and talk about that year. But when this year finally passed and nothing happend, it begins feel uninportant what this game might have told you.
Instead, it's 1986, a remider that this is only a story. A story you listen to while you play. It doesn't matter that the world is going to end SOMEDAY, it only matters that in the universe of Deadlight, the world is already dead.
Everyone who appreciates good games, here it is. It will be one of the best games you've ever played. Even if its playtime doesn't lasts long (about 3 hours), it will be an unforgetable event. Sit back, close the windows, lock yourself up and enjoy Deadlight. You won't regret it.

-It pays to spray in close quarters

This is without question one of the best medieval games ever made. Fans of the medieval genre will love this game. Why? Because it has everything one would love to do! Aside from the epic battles, there's also the politics of running your own kingdom, you have to kiss people's boots if you want nobles to flock to your side.
The core gameplay is solid and stable. Basically, the player takes control of a hero they name and design, and are unleashed into the world of Caldaria which has broken up into several factions fighting for power. You need to go around paying mercenaries and soldiers to join your little band, gaining renown and honour along the way. Once you've stormed and successfully taken your first castle you become a lord. Of course your enemies won't like that. So in the end your main goal is to create a dynasty that rules over all of Caldaria. To get there, you need to slay many enemies. The combat mechanics may seem confusing to newcomers at first, but once you understand it's actually quite clear and fun. When you're in those massive battles your weapon is your best friend. The game offers many weapons, mainly swords, greatswords, lances, bows, crossbows and others. As you progress you can buy stronger and better weapons.
For some PC gamers, performance and visuals are important. The game runs smoothly, especially when there are 200 ragdolls lying about. The graphics, despite being dated, are still very nice to look at. The thing to remember is, Warband is simply the original Mount and Blade game, but with HDR textures, better sounds, animations etc...  This game is old, but still impressive.
I love this game, 9/10, if you're a fan of all things medieval this game is for you. Think of it as Total War, but you actually get to be with your troops battling it out. Since this game has full mod support there exist some great content mods. For those who are hardcore fans of Game of Thrones (like me) there exists a mod called A Clash of Kings that put you straight into Westeros... Give it a shot!
If you're looking for an authentic feeling of post-apocalyptic survival, this is it! This game plays like a slower-paced version of Left 4 Dead, and that's not a bad thing.

The zombie craze has gone full swing in recent years, permeating into just about every form of media, most prominently in video games. In just the past year, we saw the releases of The Walking Dead, Resident Evil 6, ZombiU, Lollipop Chainsaw, etc. 2013 looks no different, with the recent release of The Walking Dead: Survival Instinct and the impending releases of Dead Island: Riptide, The Last of Us, and many, many more. The market is becoming saturated by games with similar themes which, by now, feel repetitive and uninspired. In this particular instance, if a developer is intent on making a game with zombies, the least one could ask for is for it to be unique. And if you are reading this recommendation, then you are probably wondering, “Does Deadlight have what it takes to stand out?”
Deadlight is an indie title developed by Tequila Works and published by Microsoft Studios. Amidst the sea of other zombie games, this one delivers the experience as a 2.5D platformer. In terms of gameplay, it is no different from a side-scroller—only here, the background adds another layer of visual depth. While the player is limited to moving in a two-dimensional plane, ambient objects will still appear three-dimensional. This illusion helps bring the atmosphere to life with backdrops that depict shuffling zombies and crumbling buildings.
Outside the action sequences are cutscenes rendered in sketches very reminiscent of comic books. Each character looks distinct, and even with the poor voice acting, these drawings do a fantastic job of conveying emotions. All this artistic investment immensely contributes to the dark and gloomy mood of the post-apocalyptic setting.
Unfortunately, the great visuals are the only positive thing I have to say about Deadlight. Both its plot and its mechanics feel generic. The premise revolves around some protagonist, Randall Wayne, looking for his family in the aftermath of the outbreak. He, along with several companions, journey through the city and cross paths with beings they realize are more dangerous than the undead: other humans. The venture ultimately cumulates to a conclusion that is both nonsensical and laughable. Fortunately, there is an alternate ending that adds a neat little twist and puts a darker spin on the events of the game. However, unlocking this requires the player to beat Deadlight in one sitting and without deaths. How much stress this is worth is entirely up to you.
The crux of the problem, though, lies in its gameplay. There is nothing inherently wrong with it, but it lacks anything memorable. Deadlight encourages (and occasionally forces) the player to avoid confrontation despite presenting him with an arsenal of weapons. Doing so severely limits the freedom and variation in gameplay. With movement already confined to a two-dimensional plane, it might have been nice to at least give players both the options to act violently or to flee, not just the latter.
Another irritating issue I came across was jumping. Randall seems to lack the ability to jump in any direction other than straight up. Consequently, the player must be position Randall almost perfectly below a ledge if he is to grab onto it while jumping. This can be extremely rage-inducing when a horde of zombies is right on your heels.
I can see that Tequila Works tried to be different and on an artistic level, they were. Sadly, graphics are only a minor factor in the overall quality of a game. Deadlight is not a terrible game, but you shouldn’t settle for average. There are other indie games that are more deserving of your time and money. But if you really insist on having zombies and platforming, then maybe, just maybe, Deadlight is for you.
Grade: 2/5

Deadlight is an atmospheric and story-driven 2.5D zombie survival platformer that doesn't focus on the typical run-and-gun mechanics of most of the other zombie games but instead puts the spotlight on the story and the survival aspects of a zombie apocalypse.
The game is powered by the Unreal Engine, so visually the game looks pretty great for a 2.5D sidescroller. Both the visual fidelity and the detailed and lovingly crafted levels build up a nightmarish atmosphere and underlines the horror of a zombie-infested city.
I won't talk much about the story. While it isn't exactly innovative, it's the way the story is told that keeps you going on. Secrets you find across the levels give you an even deeper insight of what happened and why. Oh, and the ending comes with a pretty surprising twist...
As mentioned before, the game focuses on the survival aspect, so while you do find guns in the game, you rather rarely find ammo for them and mostly end up using the guns to shoot padlocks or other 'puzzle' elements.
Gameplay-wise, Deadlight doesn't exactly re-invent the wheel and comes with the typical platforming and combat controls. There are no special moves, whacky weapons or the likes, so it's all pretty much basic platformer-101.
Since this is a platformer, there is a lot of, uh, platforming going on. Most of the time not really challenging, you come across a couple parts where things can get quite frustrating, e.g. where you have to escape a collapsing building and stuff like that. Luckily enough, the checkpoints are placed pretty well, so you rarely end up having to re-play a large chunk of the level in order to get back to where you died, but still, I feel like a bit more fine-tuning wouldn't have hurt the platforming aspect of the game.
According to the ingame stats, it took me 06h46m to beat the game. That involved 100%-ing the game (finding all secrets and bonuses), quite a bit of trial-and-error and a whole lot of dying. Personally, I think that's pretty much the right length for a game like this but it surely can be beaten in 5 hours or less if you don't care about finding the secrets and don't die as often as I did... :D
So, Deadlight won't exactly win any innovation awards, but it certainly approaches the zombie genre from a slightly different direction than the typical zombie-slaugher games, which works out really well. Together with the solid platforming mechanics and the gripping story-telling, Tequila Works managed to release a detailed and pretty impressive debut game, so one can hope they keep up the quality for a possible sequel.
Definitely worth checking out!

Please note that this Early Access review is not a substitute for a comprehensive bug report.
Contagion is the zombie game purists have been waiting for since they first cracked open "The Zombie Survival Guide".
For me, that's about ten years. For ten years I've waded through a horde of zombie games. Nothing emulated the raw feeling of isolation and cold that a gunshot in the distance or a scream or absolute silence can bring. We're all familiar with Brooks' original canon for zombies. Only headshots kill them. Eat flesh until they can't. Only sensory organs that have not been decayed or destroyed work. A moan causes others to moan, and they are attracted to the sound like a foghorn in the night. I never felt like I would truly find the zombie game that emulated this canon so perfectly. First there was Dead Rising - a close contender - followed by Dead Space [which opened a whole new can of worms] and Dead Island, which underperformed in basically every aspect. Left 4 Dead left a hollow feeling, mowing down thousands of zombies in a few hours seemed not worthwhile. Even DayZ left a bitter taste with its focus on player interaction and intense PVP, zombies were a secondary addition to the game and in their state of bugginess and all-out failure to function were hardly a threat to be feared for all but the newest players.
Finally, though, finally. From the ashes of Zombie Panic! Source comes a developer prepared to emulate and yet transform the genre. Erasing waypoints with Google Maps on a cell phone and slaughtering the idea of overpowered zombies by balancing their frailty with disguise and scarce ammo, this game is reaching for the stars.
Contagion performs in ways I never thought I would see, genuinely. It strikes feelings of sudden and intense panic, a moan can send my heart pounding in my ears, praying it would be silent so I could hear which direction the zombie was coming from. A gunshot can bring hell's fury itself down on your head, while boarding up windows and doors can buy you time to escape. Zombies' interaction with the world largely seems to be directed by line of sight and various audio cues, which gives them a shambling and confused appearance. A slight trigger can send Zack coming at you, but a bullet in the wrong place can mean a bite, and a risk of infection. Incentivized by kill count and bragging rights, a human infected is unlikely to share this information with his teammates for fear of being shot on the spot. A group of humans prepared to fight off a horde of 50+ shambling corpses can easily be dissuaded by a misaligned headshot tearing off the jaw of a zombie and inspiring panic in the squad. A misplaced shotgun round can result in legless zombies crawling under the horde and into your lines. Brutality, free-for-all, and all out panic. All of it rings true of the first days of the Zombie apocalypse, and all of it brings a warm feeling of nostalgia to my heart, and hopeful eyes for the bright future where the Zombie genre isn't filled with crafting games, 8-bit indie♥♥♥♥♥♥ and quick time events.
Even the zombie player gameplay has merits. A helpfully designed "camouflage" button allows an inept player to disguise himself as he views his zombie in the third person and have control assumed by the AI. Moaning loudly can draw a horde, and in turn the moans of those zombies draw more, which can be lead to the human's hideouts and used to swarm them. A biting function has a high chance to infect humans, and watching your former counterparts murder each other for fear of infection in their hideout is rewarding in its own regard.
I've never been so happy to realize a game was early access. After about 30-40 hours, I can easily see myself growing tired with this title and passing it into novelty, but it was well worth the 3$ spent. Call me nostalgia-blind, but there's so much potential content to see from these developers, and I'm very excited to be along for the ride.

I've spent so many hours in Warband that it stopped being funny, then resumed to be hilarious again.
Mount and Blade: Warband is literally one of those games that you can play almost however you want. It has a HUGE following of modders on the game forums and because the graphics are so low (designed for Direct X 7 and 9) you can have battles filled with a potentially massive amount of AI troops.  However If you don't want to field tons of troops all at once in a battle, and prefer want a small band of heroes/glorified serial killers that can slay foes in millions (IE every battle scene involving Aragorn, Legolas, Gimli or Gandalf in The Lord of the Rings.) You can do that easily by scaling down the max-battle size and recruit handful of troops or companions found in the game by traveling to each city's inn.
The combat design itself is very simple yet fantastic, and offers a high skill curve. The game by default gives you a few training wheels to use that you can turn off to experience warband in a much more raw, skill intensive way. (Practicing becomes a must if you want to turn them off and have fun, I'd recommend it however.)
Note: Training wheels are more or less disabled in multiplayer.
The AI in the game is rudimentary, simple and scripted. Mods can flush out new behavior from troops or map-characters but even in vanilla it's still great, only having a few glaring flaws. Castle/Town sieges are one of them, melee defenders only sit up on walls with their archer buddies until an attacking force comes up the ladders. Castle gates during battles don't really have a point in vanilla, since you can't interact with them in any way to change the circumstances in battle (this isn't true in multiplayer.)
The campaign itself is pretty variable, I've had playthroughs start where one or two certain factions were clearly dominating only to find them being absolutely slaughtered in the next start.
Starting out has some interesting customizability that tries to give you a reasonable  in the world. Social Class comes greatly into play with your starting point. You can start out as a lowly urchin who is born into a legacy of peniless thieves or you can start out as a noble or a wealthy trader and have some initial standing or money, and so on. There are plenty of choices to pick from. Gender bias also comes into play, but to a very small degree, and only at the start.

+ fun core gameplay
the bad:
- story has some major plotholes / inconsistencies
- I'd have preferred more action (a la Shadow Complex). I'd say the game is 95% platforming, 5% action
- gameplay is often trial&error, which I don't like in storydriven games. Fortunately, loadtimes are short and there are many checkpoints.
