- no replayability
Conclusion: I'd say it's worth it at the <$5 pricepoint.

Canadian zombie platformer parkor ranger.
This is a solid 3-5 hours of game.  It's a gorgeous little run and jump survival horror.  Your character motions are very fluid and, despite the amazing physical leaps your 35-year old park ranger does, feels very human.  The controls are very sticky and forgiving, it's rare you have to make a jump *just so*.  Autosave points are very, very common so you rarely have to replay much because of a stupid mistsake.
Like good survival horror, you want to avoid getting into a fight.  Often you don't even have a weapon.
It's extremely linear and there is usually only one way to solve any puzzle.  That's forgiven by a good story, voice acting, the puzzles being easy to the point of highlighting the next thing to interact with and it being mercifully short.  If you're not ok with a very linear game, forget it.
Most of the game gives you a very good sense of urgency without actually rushing you.  Whether it's a horde of zombies right behind you, running away from helicopters shooting at you, or bits of building that collapse just after you've left them.  This starts to break down at the end of the game with a handful of scenes which require split second reactions and memorizing traps, but for the most part they do a good job.

When it comes to FPS, several features determine whether the game is a huge hit or brushed off as another FPS.

- Customisation on loadout/class
- Ability to bring in several classes of the same faction (Provided if you purchase additional starter infantry with gold or Academy trained soldiers with credits)

Negative Points:
- Matchmaking is HUGELY UNBALANCED in Tier 2 matching.

Still on the whole, it is a good game. Remember, FPS are all about game concept and playability, though having prices reduced on equipments will defnitely help to enhance gameplay.

Mount and Blade Warband is an amazing game, and personally one of my favorites of all time. It's unique because it mixes battle strategy with you actually fighting as your own character in them, giving orders on the battlefield. The setting is Calradia, a land of which 6 factions fight for dominance. There is always some war being fought. You can aid these factions, help a claimant to the throne rebel, or become a king and try to conquer all of Calradia. Lords, towns, villages, and factions all have seperate relations with you, affecting how you interact with them to some degree. If you choose to aid a faction and become a sworn vassal, you get to own land, however, the king will probably give you a recently looted village to start with. There's even multiplayer, with various gamemodes to choose from. The above mentioned features are only a part of what this game has to offer, so I suggest you give it a try and discover what Mount and Blade Warband has to offer for yourself!

So I'm finally writing a review for Warband, one of the best games I've played for the longest time. 4 years now and I'm still coming back, but the thing is, I'm not playing the vanilla game. Oh no, this is one of the most mod-friendly games out there. The vanilla game is good, yes, I enjoyed it the first time I played, but mods just improve it so much that there really is no point to play the vanilla version again.
Basically, in this game you got to become the ruler of the land. In vanilla, the land is called Calradia and you are destined to rule it. You make your character, pick your history and then basically start out as nobody. The world is open to you, you can be anyone in this game. A trader, a mercenary, a bandit, an explorer, a vassal to a monarch, but the path leads to one thing - becoming a ruler yourself.
Also, there are mods which don't require you to become a ruler of anything, mods which are just open world battles, adventures, roleplaying or all of them combined.

Okay, where do i begin?
This is an early access game.
That much is for sure but don't let that deceive you into thinking this game isn't good.
It has so much potential and with that in mind, play it without thinking of the other games that have come before it (Left 4 Dead 1-2, Killing Floor, etc.) so that you'll experience it as the devs intended. I like how they decided to make ammunition scarce, making the experience almost like real life. You are not likely to find a gun and a ton of ammo next to it behind a desk in real life. Well unless you're in a gun shop but i digress..
The stamina meter system forces players to pace themselves in order to survive as you would in a zombie apocalypse scenario.
Lastly, this game was meant to be played in Co-op. Playing it alone to practice is utterly boring, it would be better to play it with friends and gradually learn how to survive rather than do it on your own.
For an early access game it is really really good. I enjoyed playing, surviving, dying and shooting in the game and i'd play it again as soon as my friends are free to do so as well.

Awful PC Port
COD: Ghosts is just another Call of Duty game. The singleplayer is bad, but the multiplayer is fun to jump into now and then and doesn't require much thought or strategy. It's the kind of game that you can jump into for a short amount of time and stop playing whenever you want. Camping is a big problem in this game however, which might ruin some players' experiences. You might encounter some hackers but it's quite easy to report them.
Back to the campaign, the story is ridiculous and is hard to follow (not really worth it anyway). Basically all of South America invades the US by shooting it with giant missiles from space... you get the point. That being said, it is still fun to occasionally control some ridiculous weapon attached to a helicopter to mow down tons of enemies.
The real reason I wouldn't recommend this game on PC is the how bad the port is. The graphics don't look much better than the console version. Framerates aren't good either. It dips below 30 fps on my rig (which gets around 50 fps in Battlefield 4, a far better looking game). There's one attachable sight that makes the game go to around 5 fps (not intentionally). To conclude, if you do want to get this game, get it on a console.

I have to grudgingly recommend this because of the excellent stealth gameplay and realistic level design, despite uplay and one of the stupidest plots ever written for a video game. Some highlights:
Our protagonist meets his friend, who has an escape plan:
"How will we escape?"
"We found a boat!"
"Awesome!"
"A broken boat."
"I... uh... guess you could fix it..."
"A broken boat in a cave at the top of a mountain."
"What?"
"A cave with no boat-sized exits..."
"Seriously?"
"...or any nearby water."
(long pause)
"How many of those pills did you take?"
"Eleventy?"
"Yeah, that's what I thought..."
Our protagonist meets up with Buck, who has been sending him to uncover ancient lost tombs:
"Listen, Buck. The last two times you sent me to a 'lost' tomb, it was filled with pirates. Not centuries-old ghost pirates - the normal kind. And when I got there, you were already there waiting for me. I'd guess that both you and every pirate on the island already knows where the stupid tomb is. So instead of using this magic stone compass thing, why don't we try looking for the tomb on a tourist map first?"
Our protagonist meets up with Buck one last time:
"Hey Buck"
"Hey, Snow White. I'm here to betray you."
"That was incredibly obvious. Do you realize that I'm holding a small arsenal?"
"Yep."
"...and that I killed like 200 dudes on the way here?"
"Yep."
"...and that all you have is a dull antique knife, and you're standing on the other side of the room?"
"Yep."
"Then why tell me?"
"Because you can't shoot me during a cutscene."
"Touche."
Our protagonist meets a deep cover agent:
"Hey I've got a plan to kill Hoyt."
"Hit me."
"First we'll bring you to his private office and introduce you to him. You'll try to get a job working for him, and after we've earned his trust we'll get you an invitation to one of his poker games. You can kill him when you're alone with him at the game."
"Wait... this plan starts with meeting Hoyt alone, then follows an elaborate set of steps so we can... uh... meet with Hoyt alone?"
"Exactly."
"I can't think of a problem with that. Let's go."
Our protagonist is presented with a moral choice at the end of the game:
"Jason, you must choose to leave the island with your friends, or kill them and stay here with me."
"You want me to do what to my friends?"
"Kill them."
"Sorry, I thought you said kill them."
"I did."
"Not even if you weren't obviously a psychopath. Nobody would kill their friend for no reason. Actually, nobody would even have lifted the knife to her throat unless a cutscene made them do it. Why would you even include this as an option? Seriously, who thought this ending was worthy of occupying space on my hard disk? Hold on a second. Let me Google this."
Jason puts down the knife and pulls out his phone.
"Wait..." he giggles "the main writer thought this plot was clever? Oh my goodness." he starts laughing "the guy thinks that he's subverting video game cliches by just retelling them in the most literal way? Hahaha. Oh this is good. He said in an interview that he thinks we should be looking for deeper meanings rather than just saying 'I get it. That was dumb.' That would be like looking for deeper meanings in Earnest Goes to Camp. He honestly thinks critics hate this plot because we only half-listened to it, not because we understood it and think it's idiotic."
Jason ghasps for breath and wipes a tear from his eye.
Citra stares at him for a moment. "So... uh... are you going to kill your friends?"
"No, but thanks for the laughs."
"Wait! What will you do now?"
"Steal some cars and sneak into a bunch more heavily armed compounds because - honestly? That's a riot."

Escape: If you've played any of the original Zombie Panic: Source modification, you know escape mode. You and a number of friends play as human suvivors (for now) of a zombie outbreak, having just retreated into the lobby of a deserted and overrun metropolitan police facility and you have to work together and make your escape from the building. Along the way you scavenge for ammunition, tools and supplies to help you overcome the challenges of the facility. As your friends fall, they turn into Alpha Zombies, able to sprint, climb, and jump with abilities normally outside the capability of a Zombie (more akin to a 28 Days Later infected, or an Alien in AvP). Able to access some areas inaccessable to the human players, the quest for survival becomes more difficult as time goes, and the number of Alpha Zombies rises and surpasses that of the remaining humans. The escape route is randomized, keeping the map fresh for many play throughs.
Hunt Mode: A well done tense stalking simulation, where you and a number of friends begin as humans scattered amidst a zombie infested suburban community, cul-de-sacs and all, or a quarantine research tent complex deployed in a local municipal park. Each round you must outlast the rest of the players to be the last one alive, whether through pacifist evasion, cooperative efforts, or active negation (killing the other humans Hunger Games/Running Man style) - and as the players fall, they become alpha zombies, just as in escape, making the game progressively harder as time goes on.
Two key factors of both the above modes is that the maps themselves are large (in the virtual square footage sense) and structurally randomized in some sense, doors / pathways open in one round may be blocked, locked or closed off in the next - fires and other phenomenon are randomized somewhat as well - keeping the levels fresh for many play throughs. Additional, resource placement (ammo, weapons, tools), is randomized throughout the level as well - the shotgun you found on the receptionists floor may not be there the next time.
Contagion uses the Source engine as well, so the movement and feel of the game is on par with other Source games I've played, keep that in mind if you're finicky about those things.
My Wishes:
1) While there certainly would be work involved in rebooting and refining a dozen or so maps available for Zombie Panic: Source, I think the effort should be made. I remember several that were quite excellent that I'd like to see make the jump into new & revised Contagion versions, especially with some of the new mechanics granting the classics some new (undead?) life.
2) There needs to be a mechanism to allow unlimited & a selectable number of zombie respawns in Escape mode - sometimes when the randomizer hands the humans a large amount of ammunition and better weaponry early in the map it's impossible for a small number of player zombies (if any humans die at all) to provide much challenged to a well armed troupe.
3) There needs to be voting mechanisms for the usual - key settings, map change, kicking offending players, etc.
I haven't played much of the third mode, Extraction, where you must help Counter-Strike-esque "Survivors" (I still call them hostages on VOIP in game half the time) hold out in a house until extraction arrives, then escort the survivors to the extraction point, and then a new house gets chosen with more surivors, repeat. As in the other modes, as players die they become Alpha Zombies, making it more difficult to protect the AI survivors. The zombies seem to swarm the hold out point, so a successful strategy I've seen a lot use it to sprint in quick, get the hostages, er survivors to follow you, then run out of the house with them to another part of the neighborhood until the extraction arrives. As the survivors escape, they toss out a pittance of ammunition and the occasional weapon. Since you can only enter the house activated as the hold out point, equipping is rough with a full set of eight or more players, and the escaping survivors don't provide enough resupply (by far) for the mode. I don't know if there's a fixed number of survivors to rescue, or if it just keeps going until all the players / survivors die - just haven't played enough to know.

I didn't finish it yet, but i had to write this review since it has such a high score that makes me think that i need to warn you about it:
Sometimes it wants you to think, other times to be frenetic and say "♥♥♥♥ Everything And Run", but what fails about it is that it does that in the wrong places, or both situations are combined where it ends up causing your death.
For example, (SPOILERS) you're running from a helicopter through an office building, at a floor of the complex the main character says "If those spotlights see me, i'm screwed" . I was supposed to stop, and lure a zombie (Who was in the background, mind you) to get to the lights so he would walk away. Problem being, i was already running from the helicopter at that point before he even said the line, since by instinct i was running away from it, like i was 3 minutes ago, and then it shot me and i died. I think this game has a lot of moments like that.
The combat is kind of a gamble, you have an axe which allows you to fight zombies, but to be able to kill them you have to attack them while they're on the floor, fallen. To do that, you need to hit them a couple of times prior to it. This becomes a problem in chase scenes, because you have zombies behind you, and in front of you. To escape from the ones behind, you need to make the ones in the front fall by using your axe, or they block your path. Problem being, sometimes you get an instant kill with your first hit, another time they take like 6 hits before they fall so you're able to get away from them.
(TLDR) What i'm getting at is, the frustration of dying to not having lightning reaction times, didn't get used to the controls in the first half hour (And they're still making you learn more) , or that you don't know between running away, think, or do both, make this game NOT enjoyable. The scenes that you don't die at that are really fast paced, they end up feeling very good, but most of them are ruined by the problems i mentioned.

There are some small puzzles in the game, but nothing overly difficult and some of the areas are more trial and error than anything else. The fighting in the game is solid, but sometimes basically running past zombies and getting to the next area is your best bet since your character doesn't take too many hits before dying.
Overall, it's a decent game that could've been better especially in length, but a solid platformer worth trying out.

This should have been a great game.
The action is fun and natural and the game introduces new stuff often enough not to turn combat into a chore. The islands are nice both up close and from afar (which is a rather important thing, given the amount of time you'll be spending airborne). Too bad Ubisoft decided to turn the main storyline into a steaming pile of refuse.
The single enjoyable character is a bats*it insane methhead of a villain who dies halfway through the story in the single most underwhelming boss fight ever (press button to do stuff in a cutscene, WOW GEE THANKS, I really missed that plague of a stupid mechanic unleashed upon the gaming scene by Modern Warfare or who the hell even did it first). The rest of the characters, including the protagonist, are annoying, irredeemable idiots.
Ubisoft spastically tries to be the cool kid on the block who subverts all of the gaming stereotypes, but they just aren't very good at it. Calling players out on killing people has long since outlived its novelty, especially if you aren't given any choice. In the end they basically ask you outright whether you're a terrible person or not. Wow, Ubisoft. Deep stuff.
To add insult to injury, the game is riddled with small annoyances that break up the otherwise fun island action. Yes, I know there's a main story to progress, there's no need to replay that god*amn same conversation EVERY SINGLE TIME I reload a save, or even just switch back from a sidequest (just as bland and forgettable as the main storyline - or your money back). The HUD is obtrusive and babies the player way too much.
Several of the game mechanics go unused because of their stupid implementation. Real cool that I can use like, ten types of combat drugs and special arrows and whatnot, too bad I have FOUR quick use slots I can assign them to, ALL of which are already occupied, so using any of them will replace other, usually more useful actions. And alternate takedowns? There wasn't a single opportunity where I could have plausibly used the death-from-below skill, let alone the double version. Oh, and the save system is cancer, too.
All in all, this really could have been a great game, if only the gameplay would be paired with something that would stitch the hundreds of enjoyable gunfights, rides, flights and hunts together to create a coherent game, not just a collection of disjointed fun. Still, it's more than worth it for the couple bucks Far Cry 3 will cost you on a sale these days.

Deadlight is one of those games that feels like a marriage of the old and new. The old being the Prince Of Persia (Pre-Sands of Time) running, climbing and jumping around in a 2d environment. While the "new" part, is the kind of story that's being  told and partly the melee/gunplay elements.
If there's anything disappointing about Deadlight, it's the length of the game. I had no problem playing through, from beginning to finish, within a little over 4 hours of play. So, longevity, it ain't got! I also thought the story kind of ended abruptly. And the "Nightmare mode" that gets unlocked on completion of the game doesn't make me want to re-play it.
On the other hand, there are extras to look through, e.g. artwork, behind the scenes videos, etc. that will be nice to view. Still, I got it in a sale for cheap, and I throroughly enjoyed the game. It's a beautiful looking game with a horror backdrop and the gameplay felt almost, 'just right.' However, it has slight "jump when I don't want to" issues along with some slightly iffy voice acting. But again, the rest of the game raises it above these minor issues.
Overall, I'd buy it again. A great experience and a lot of fun to play through. But, that said, the full price is not worth it. With just over 4 hours of play, it's not enough at that price. Get it at a fiver or less and you'll be pleased.

This game is simply one of the best "zombie apocalypse" multiplayer I've ever had.
It mixes a litlte bit of realism with a little bit of fast paced gameplay. The game contains good puzzles in the escape maps, and it requires a good level of cooperation on the extraction maps.
Ammo isn't avaliable anywhere, so make any of your shots count, and don't forget to share it with your comrades. This has made this game pretty neat.
But hey, now there is the PVP mode. One thing that annoyed me in the past zombie games/mods, was the PVP. One team of humans vs zombies. Just that. Humans could get to high places and spam M4A1 shots on them, making it impossible for zombies to reach, but in Contagion, this is different. The PVP mode is a mix of FFA with a VS and King of the Hill Mode. You have to kill the other players in order to survive, and be advised, all the players begin as humans. Killed some of them? Nice! But watch out, because they will come back from hell as reanimated corpses and hunt you down, and this is one of the best parts on this game: Humans. Are. Not. O.P against the zombies. This little fact over here made this game one of the best Multiplayer experiences I had on 2013, and it will be one of the best of 2014.

I was reluctant to start this game at first. A sidescrolling post-apocalyptic game? Didn’t sound like it would be all that great to me. I changed my mind after about five minutes of play. I don’t know how they crammed so much atmosphere into a sidescroller, but they did. And for a sidescrolling game, the graphics have incredible depth to them. Zombies do not just come from your left and right, but they emerge from the background as well, slowly shambling to the foreground as you attempt to complete some puzzle, putting the pressure on., it makes for a very tense experience. The downside to this game is the sloppy control. Unlike Mark of the Ninja which had the slickest, tightest control in any platforming sidescroller I've ever played, Deadlight is a bit sludgy, particularly with moves like the rebound jump and when you are trying to jump over walls. The difficulty also ramps up too high too fast toward the end for my tastes. But, after all the cussing from the last third of the game was over, I would still recommend this title. A solid story, gorgeous visuals and fantastic atmostphere.

2.5D games have been recently making their way into the gaming landscape and Deadlight puts a zombie/post-apocalypse twist in an attempt to put itself apart from the rest. With Amazon having a great deal a little while ago I just couldn't pass up the chance to try it out.
Set in 1986 Seattle after a global event that plunged the world into chaos and destroyed most of life on earth. Playing as Randall Wayne, a man looking for his friends and family and bring them to safety, the player must avoid the Shadows, a zombie like foe that plagues the game, and also battle the living that are trying to survive as well.
Deadlight has a dark story but borrows heavily from major zombie movies that one can almost guess it while playing and really is hard to feel compelled to finish the game. The cinematic scenes are really the only thing that kept me going as it's motion graphics was like Metal Gear Solid: Digital Graphic Novel which were quite interesting.
The game is also dark to give the feel of dread with the graphics being styled with grit and the gameplay limiting the player with either limited resources or nothing but to have the player run for safety. The only problem is that sometimes the game put the player in tough situations that cause more frustration than enjoyment with Shadows swarming before the player can do anything or being unable to do basic platforming to get away.
The sounds and FX are basic suspenseful tracks and zombie moans but the most annoying thing is the cinematic scenes are not adjustable and blasted out my speakers with little warning.
I love the post-apocalypse settings and was very interested in Deadlight when I heard about it but after hearing that it wasn't that great of a game I hesitated. And after playing, the review were not unfounded and Deadlight should only be bought by post-apocalypse fans and only when on sale.

Buy this game if you have no wish to be a productive human being. Once you get over the butt ugly interface the game sucks you in with its extremely satisfying combat (Imagine charging past an archer on your steed, swinging your sword low and hearing the sickening crunch of sword on flesh followed by a strangled scream... ).
But beneath the seemingly simple combat is a layer of complexity that is intiutive and easy to grasp. 4 Directions to block and 4 directions to attack from, with speed and direction of attack factoring in for bonuses or penalties (hit a man on the helmet, you'll give him a bad headache, hit him just under his chin where cloth meets skin and he'll crumple at your feet).
The combat is only a single layer that makes up this game. It's like a cake, and each of it's layers offers fresh challenges and experiences filled with sweetness and delight. From troop management to merchantilism to politicing and ruling kingdoms. Every layer is complementary to each other, but can be approached individually at your own pace. Obviously things like ruling requires a solid understanding of how each of the other systems work. And once your in a position to wage war against a neighbouring kingdom things begin to snowball, like sitting a final exam it will test your experience in all avenues of the game's layers.
Live your game of thrones fantasies with this game ...at least until season 5 is out.

A zombie genre take on a side-scrolling classic like Another World, Flashback and Heart of Darkness.
The plot is fairly predictable, filled with clichés and the scripting is pretty poor in quite a few places, but the game itself is worthwhile.
Set in and around Seattle in 1986, there's a lot of interesting scenery and locations. A lot of the environmental puzzles are really well designed and there's a feeling of exploring a grimly beautiful diorama.
A few of the chapters had really fun gameplay elements, but felt like they were completely un-needed for the story. The game has a 'twist', and quite a modest attempt at putting a lot of thought behind it all, especially in the form of diary pages, which you find as you explore. However, this level of the story requires quite a lot of patience reading through the pages you find.
The game has a well implemented checkpoint feature, respawning you generally just a few moments before you made your fatal error. Each scene is a puzzle and the game generally doesn't punish you for making a mistake. I did encounter a couple of moments where I was set back about a minutes worth of gameplay, which felt frustrating but only by comparison to how good the system usually was.
Overall, good clichéd fun and an interesting merge of gameplay and genre.

I really wanted to like this game. Unfortunately, there is a lot of frustration included with this sometimes entertaining game. This is one of the best looking 2.5d game I've seen. It's up there with Trine 2 and Insanely Twisted Shadow Planet. It looks very realistic. The backgrounds are lively and there's always lots of stuff going on.  The voice actor for the grizzled main character did a good job. This game's best feature is its style. That's about all it has going for it, though. The actual gameplay is thin. Standard platforming. Jump here, climb that. Run. Duck. Wail away on a zombie. It can be entertaining, but nothing that hasn't been done before. The controls are decent for most of the scenarios encountered in the game, but at times when quick precision is necessary, the  game falls flat on its face. At times the pace of the game grinds down to a screeching halt as parts need to be played over and over and over again due to the controls not responding properly. There's also other times where you have a split second to react to things or else death. Sometimes there's no way to know what exactly is being asked until dying and restarting the section again.  The very ending of the game nicely encapsulates all the shortcomings I've just listed. I see promise from the developers, but this game just does too many things poorly to recommend.

Updated review, I've played this for a while now and recently came back to it after 6 months or so.  From the hours played, you can probably tell I've got my money's worth.  I'm not sure what all the whining on here is about.
It's 100% accurate that there are not a lot of players for the game online.  There are about 50% fewer players than when I played it before.  However, for the most part the players that have been on there have been decent.  Generally, the fewer the players, the more cooperation you get as in ammo exchange and help.
As far as development, I came back after 6 months and the game does have a couple more player models, more guns, more game modes and added maps.  So, it doesn't seem like the developer is sitting back and doing nothing.  I also dont rate a game based on developer hate, I just judge it on if the game has had new things added to it.  It has.
They may need to evaluate some of the maps, because as others have noted, there are some issues with some opf them.  I noticed on the mansion escape map that players can hide behind a shop light in the attic and no one/zombies can really get to them.  That's an easy enough fix, just remove the shop light from the attic.
I mentioned this a year ago and I still believe that there needs to be some sort of visual indication of what type of ammunition you are carrying.  I think this would give a visual clue that players (especially new ones- yes they are out there!) need to drop ammo they can not use for other players.  Either that, or the ammo they have horded should start to weigh them down somehow.
If you buy the game on sale and play it for a while, I think it's well worth the money.  I've played it a long time and will continue to play it on and off.  I've had a lot of fun cooperating with others on escape (Although IT IS much more fun with two or three players than with eight) and hunting down other players while dodging zombies on Hunted.
Is it as smooth and polished as Left for Dead 2?  No way, but it is a different type of game.  Contagion is creepier and slower than Left for Dead and I would say the paths are not as forced (which obviously leads to confusion and occasional panic).
I still recommend this one on sale.

Deadlight's biggest appeal is its great visual style and atmosphere. Everything looks excellent and there's a good amount of depth to each location to help break up the 2D side-scroller feel. You play a character named Randall, who's been separated from his friends and family and is looking for them. The storyline is pretty throw-away. Around the 2/3 mark the game really starts to lose steam and resorts to some pretty cheap instant death traps and timed segments that rely on precision jumping skills. Unfortunately, the game's controls aren't quite as precise as they need to be to accomplish these sections without dying repeatedly due to your character being unresponsive to your inputs. More than a few times Randall will just stay attached to a wall or fence, refusing to jump, despite the jump button being pressed repeatedly. This gets really frustrating really fast. It's a pretty short game too, only taking a few hours to complete. I'd recommend picking it up if you can get it for $5 or less. Overall, I'd give it a 6/10.

Especially after "The Walking Dead" game, there's really not a whole lot you can do with the zombie genre storytelling wise. Which is maybe why playing "Deadlight" feels kind of been there done that. There's a group of survivors, you get separated from them, you spend the game searching for your family. People heroically sacrifice themselves, or alternately, beg you to kill them so they don't become a zombie....etc, etc. All of this stuff is kind of becoming a bit cliché, especially since it's all been done so well elsewhere before this (again, "The Walking Dead"). The ending manages its own twist which is kind of nice, but most of the game up to that point is pretty underwhelming.
Gameplay wise it's basically "Prince of Persia" with zombies, but it also doesn't do much that's original with that concept. There are a few physics puzzles and annoying timed jumping sequences, but mostly it's a pretty straightforward platformer with not a whole lot that's memorable about it. And considering that I was able to beat the entire thing in 3 hours, "15 dollars" is grossly overpriced (if for some reason you really want to play this, I say wait until it's 75% off).

Deadlight is a very atmospheric story-focused zombie apocalypse platformer.  It's a bit of a mouthful but it's the best way to describe it.  The storytelling reminds me a lot of Alan Wake (minus the surrealism) and it works quite well.  There are gaps in the story that you can fill in with collectibles found along the way.  Deadlight even includes handheld electronic games you can play from the main menu after finding t hem in game which is a nice touch.
Gameplay-wise, it's semi-realistic platforming action.  By this I mean that you have fairly realistic speed, jumping abilities, ledge hanging and that sort of thing.  The platforming works very well and has a bit of fudge room so it won't matter if you're off by a couple steps.  It also has some fairly simple puzzles that require reasonable timing to solve.  You will do a fair amount of fighting with a melee weapon and some with a gun, but you can skip a lot of it since it is primarily a survival game, not a combat game.
The game's graphics are high quality and it runs quite smoothly thanks to the Unreal engine, though in parts where it zooms the camera in it definitely doesn't look as good.  The atmosphere is excellent and gives the game a nice feel to go with the story.  Lighting, weather, and other effects are used very well.
There are a few glitches, however.  The most obvious is a certain trap in act 2 and a few places in act 3 where you are supposed to solve it by sprinting through.  Every 4 or 5 times I do so, I get killed when I should have made it though.  For this reason, I highly recommend not attempting a playthrough in nightmare mode which unlocks after you beat the game as it restarts you at the beginning of the current act when you die.  It is simply too frustrating.
Overall, this game is definitely worthwhile.  I highly recommend it to anyone who likes indie games, zombie games, or platformers.

Far Cry 3 is easily one of my top picks for shooters and open-world action. The island the game takes place on is vibrant and beautiful; full of picturesque vistas of mountains and jungles that hide caves and dark secrets.
Vaas likely ranks as one of the top video game villains ever written, and this is one of the cons with the game. The villains and other characters are written quite well and have their own unique personality, but it sometimes feels like those characters had been given more time during development than the player's character Jason Brody.
Taking outposts and exploring can take up more time than playing the missions in the game, and climbing radio towers to fill in the map was a great addition. Speaking of, while the map is more interactive in Far Cry 3, the fact it pauses the game has always been a very minor downside for me; mainly because I loved holding onto the map while still able to move and drive in Far Cry 2. How players use their melee weapon has been changed as well, and given a more Call of Duty style control to it. It's no longer a selectable weapon like your primary, secondary, or special weapon, but this has freed up that slot to allow players to carry a fourth weapon, which is a win-win for the player.
Thick foliage and better indicators of when enemies can see you and if they know you're a threat have greatly increased the ability to conduct stealth-based gameplay, and I've yet to find more fun that taking an outpost with only a bow and my knife -- raining hell with a rocket launcher or portable mortar system comes pretty close though.
Now, back to the setting. The island is vibrant and lively, and on top of being hunted by crazy pirates led by Vaas, the animals that call the island home will hunt you as well. Going toe-to-toe with a tiger or bear when you're out of ammo after taking out a pirate convoy is pretty heart-pounding, and the button-mashing/quick-time sequences when these animals are holding onto you or seconds from mauling you are intense. The moments in the water are even more intense as sharks and crocodiles hide out of sight until they see you or you're on top of them. I can't count how many times I jumped off a cliff or bridge into a river to get away from the human enemies, only to land near a croc and have it latch on and attempt a death-roll.
Aside from these there's also a couple stories hidden under Jason Brody's. One of these is the Japanese occupation during World War II, told through the old artillery positions, bunkers, and through the Letters of The Lost; collectible letters that never got sent off the island by some of the Japanese soldiers. The other, which ties into Jason Brody's story, is that of the island's natives, and brings me to my only real gripes about the game. The story of the natives is interesting, but there's some supernatural stuff in that mythology that doesn't stay myth; it's neat, but after Far Cry 2, I've never felt like Far Cry 3 or 4's supernatural sides really fit the series properly.
The other gripe is how the natives interact with Jason Brody. They help him, and ask for his help. Why do I see this as a problem? Well, it's simply because ALL of the island's problems have been caused by white people, so the natives' prophecy BS aside, it doesn't make a lot of sense for them to not only accept the help of a white man, but to also ask for it. Which brings me to my final point; Jason Brody's progress from scared rich kid to gun-toting badass. It simply happens too quickly for someone who's never had any kind of military training and probably hasn't had to work a day in their life. However, this likely happened because it would get annoying really fast for players to have their gun shaking around and unable to get a clean shot on anything, so from that perspective it makes sense, but from the story's perspective, it doesn't -- unless you just decide that the reason is "he's a fast learner".
TL;DR: This game's freakin' great, has very few flaws that can't be overlooked, has very well written villains, and a stunning game world filled with both animal and human life.

Mount & Blade Warband has terrible enemy AI, broken siege mechanics, very dated graphics, and is quite possibly one of the best games of it's kind.
Never before have I seen a game that blends RPG and Real Time Strategy together in such a satisfying way. This is emergent gameplay at it's finest because it in no way limits you from choosing to play as you see fit. You can rise to become King of the entire world and unite them all, or undermine them all by playing them against one another in a never ending conflict, or ignore war altogether to become a trader, or a bandit, maybe even take over a castle as an illegitimate marauder and see how long you can hold out against the vast armies out to take it from you. You can travel with a huge army or a small group of interesting NPCs. Don't like the base setting? You can download mods to play in real world settings, or fantastical places like Westeros from A Song of Ice and Fire, or Middle Earth from Lord of the Rings.
If you like sandbox games, this is it at it's finest. Does it have problems? Sure, of course it does. The saving grace however is that everything else works beautifully.
COMBAT - While the AI is incredibly stupid to the point of just knowing basic "charge at you screaming" tactics and turning their back to a cavalry charge to chase one guy who broke through their lines first... the combat itself is very well done. Melee feels very intense and reactionary, you have to be on your guard at all times and be ready to take advantage of any enemy weaknesses. Archery is both deadly and difficult, and requires a serious investment for your character to be good at. Unit types are varied with no one faction sharing identical unit types. Mounted combat is the best I've ever seen in a game allowing you to use a large variety of weapons from horseback and giving serious advantage to mounted warriors. There's a lot I could say about combat but it's really got to be experienced first hand.
POLITICS - With 6 main factions in the game, rival claimants to every throne, independent troops of bandits, raiders, deserters, and the like, and the possibility to even create your own separate faction, there is a ton of variety in the game. You can side with any of the factions or none of them, you can even play several off on each other if you have good relations with multiple lords. You can marry a huge number of eligible partners, as either male or female. You can even convince certain lords to defect to your own faction if they like you well enough. You can rise in influence by doing quests, conquering enemy settlements, capturing rival lords, and defending your faction's territory.
SIEGE - Siege mechanics are a little lacking, you will only ever have one ladder (which is really a ramp) or one siege tower for any castle siege, the AI again is very basic, the archers fire from a distance but all melee and cavalry units (who dismount for the siege) just clambor up single file to the top of a wall to fight a war of numbers against a swarm of bunched together units at the top. You can issue commands to pre-defined groups (Archers, Melee, Cavalry, Etc.) to tell them where to go, what kind of weapons to use, and so on, but by and large the sieges aren't the biggest highlight though they are still incredibly intense due to awesome combat mechanics.
ROLEPLAY - While there is an element of backstory and lore to this world, mostly explored through your companion's musings on areas, by and large the world is very open for interpretation. The six factions are based off real-world equivalents like the Cossacks, Mongols, Arabs, Vikings, and Gauls both in terms of unit types and archtitecture. Roleplaying shines however in how it allows you to be whoever you want to be. You can choose to start as a lord with enough honor to have your own banner sigil, or start as a lowly thief who just runs about burning villages and trying to keep one step ahead of the law as you try and make it rich. There's so many variables that let you choose how to play the game, you can even solo the game if you want for a true challenge. There are a lot of unique stats and skills you upgrade independently that affect everything from your persuasion attemps, battle tactics, map speed, weapon skill, and the size of your army.
ACTIVITIES - Aside from combat, there are quest opportunities available in villages, towns, and from other lords who ask favors. There's maybe only 10 types of quests, that range from delivering trade goods, cattle steering, bandit hunting, village defense, soldier training, attacking enemy settlements, or capturing rival lords. In addition to this there are arenas and tournaments that allow you to bet on yourself as you fight in a host of games. Upgrading buildings in towns and villages you own. Exploring towns and castles. Attending feasts. Recruiting and training units. There's always SOMETHING to do.
Bottom line, if you haven't played this game yet and you are even remotely interested in RPGs or RTSs then you need to get it now!

As far as Early Access games go, Contagion is more or less a bug free, and fairly polished experience. It's just missing something. Alot of somthings. A huge amount of somethings.
So far, the Beta offers 3 game modes, Escape, Hunt and Exctraction, all of which are excatly what it says on the tin. And out of all of these, none of them actually require teamwork, strategy or survival. For a game that does brand itself as a survival experience, there is no surviving to be done, other than kill zombies and don't get your brains blown out by your team mates. So unlike Zombie Panic: Source, weight and being outnumbered are no longer issues. You can literally kill off an entire horde by yourself, without using pr0 MLG SkiLLz. So far I have had one team-like experience, which was later ruined by my team-mate blasting my head all over the floor with a Hunting Rifle.
However, this game isn't all bad. It's very pretty, and dynamic, and lots of areas on the maps (all three of them) are accesible and can be interacted with, and they are not easily exploited. Whilst playing, I also felt some genuine panic and struggle. Sadly, not over the zombie, but more so the fact the rest of the bloodthirsty server was after me. And they were much better players. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s.
Overall, Contagion is a huge leap from Zombie Panic: Source but sadly it does not borrow enough from it. However, the game is still just in Beta and more maps, weapons and mechanincs will be added sooner or later (please, please, PLEASE.)
+ Lovely dynamic environments.

I finished the game. I bought the game during a Steam sale. I definitely got a bargain and I highly recommend this game.
I was pleasantly surprised that Far Cry 3 drew me into the story and sandbox game features. Although the "trippy" stuff was annoying, I could see the need for these "trips" to add to the story development.
Some spoilers:
- The radar towers were like jumping puzzles. Each unique, but not too crazy.
- The safari hunts were interesting, albeit annoying. Bow and arrow to hunt down 1-shot kill tigers was irritating. At least rare animals could help build your character carrying capacity.
- The combat was flexible and kept me interested. All of the camps/compounds were different in their own way. The takedown sequences were difficult to navitate due to guards no cooperating with my rock throwing. But overall, one of the best tactical semi-stealth combat games I played in a while.
- Driving is fun and the terrain challenging.
- The weapons were good, although I would have liked more silencer-type weapons near end-game.

I honestly feel that this franchise should be made into a movie because the story is just that good. Very addicting and all around fun to play FPS.

You can command your own army in person and have to actually deal with the problems of logistics, food and your own gear. It's kind of a mix between Chivalry and the Total War series, you can conquer the world and manage your towns (even your vassals) but you can do it from your character's perspective. You're no longer some sort of god that watches from space on a drawed map (which is cool too, don't get me wrong).
Now, one point is the graphics, they're really good for an indie game (made by a man and his wife) but you're going to need to mod it up a bit if you're a real graphics addict. The gameplay makes up for it ten times though!
The mods are actually a great part of the game. You have tons of them, varying from massive overhauls which completely change the financial system and more, to mods that just add some extra gear and graphics. There is so much variety. The modding community is just huge.
Some mods that I really enjoyed:
- Prophesy of Pendor (complete overhaul, new map, factions, lore, units and many more)
- Blood in the West (lord of the rings)
- Floris mod expanded (an enchancement of the current gameplay)
- Gekokujo (Samuraaaiii)

So in the first day of downloading this game i have played 4.6 hours
So this is a first day, free-to-play review. If you have ever played any other WWII shooters (Call of Dut 3 etc.) you are going to see many similarities.
Right off the bat the game looks like a reimagined Call of Duty 3 with similiar guns and open European maps, but this game captures more strategy and tactics than most Call of Dutys. And it includes fun things such as bicycles, whistling, and many vehicles and options. The guns are good and hard to use, as they should be in any skill based shooter. The maps are large and expansive with interesting enough layouts, although there are few maps in supply i enjoy all of them. This game is an Early Access Beta game so i wont nail the game on glitches and bugs. The one thing i found to be troublesome was the pay to win mentality. Leveling up is difficult unless you are very acquainted with PC FPS. And if you are like me and not a PC FPS master you will contemplate the many REAL MONEY options you can pay for to boost your performance, and collect the best guns. Now even though the game is challanging, and you are sometimes at a dissadvantage without paying for objects, i find myself having fun. Whether its tyring to capture a hardpoint and getting killed by a falling paratropper, or being run over by a crazy friend, i always seem to be having fun. Which is the most important element that sometimes gets lost in AAA titles.
I hope when this game is fully released it hosts many large expansive maps, and many weapons and options you dont have to pay more money for. I hope the developers take thes ideas into consideration, and i hope they work hard to make a great game...

How do i start a review of Far Cry 3.
First off: This is whole my opinion of the game and i don't want to change peoples minds of the game with my opinion.
THIS WILL CONTAIN SPOILERS!!
Storyline:
Storyline-wise i have to say that this game is great! The missions are really really good, you follow a guy named Jason and he is having a great time with his friends. After the intro you parachute onto an island and you get caught by a guy named Vaas. He kidnapped your friends and you need to rescue them. When you follow the storyline you will notice that there are loads of drugs used in this game, i think its very funny but some can find it offensive. You meet with loads of people spreat around the island who want to help you rescue your friends, these people can be: friends, gun dealers and people who just do not like Vaas. Later on you will find out that Vaas is not the top leader of the bad-guys. Hoyt is. He is not that crazy as Vaas but still, he is a crazy guy. The sister of Vaas wants to help you too, she helps you tho but around the finale of the storyline she will give you some trippy drugs and wants you to kill your friends. You can do that but she will kill you afterwards, she is not that nice as you might think she is. You can also kill her instead and save your friends.
Gameplay / Graphic:
The gameplay is amazing. You are in an open-world map with side-missions (i will come to that later), gunn shops and drug dealers. There are also some outposts (i will talk to that in the section *Side-Missions) The graphics are stunning and i would def. recommend it! You can also run the game on a low end pc.
Side Missions:
You also have side-missions, they contain outposts (my favorite) but also things like: shooting animals for rewards, finding animals for rewards, darting for rewards, shooting range etc etc.
Let me explain the outposts: the outposts are little camps with 5 to around 15 bad guys on it. When you kill all the bad guys (rush or stealth) you get a reward, you can loot the bodies and houses/tents and you get a little place where you find new side-missions like killing a sergeant or killing a special/rare animal. Your team will live in this camp now and no bad guys will come around in this little section.
You also have little radio-stations, you need to climb them (they are broken so its parcour) and kill the little system on the top. Then you will unlock a piece of the world on your map (before hidden but accecable) and there will be a small box with a reward in it.
So:
I really like this game and it will always stay in my heart, just like Harry Potter (books and movies) and Life if Strange.
My marks for some sections:
Storyline: 10/10 would play again
Gameplay / Graphics: 8/10
Side Missions: 9/10
PS:
Yes it has a multiplayer mode but it sucks balls. Again my opinion.

Mount & Blade Warband has terrible enemy AI, broken siege mechanics, very dated graphics, and is quite possibly one of the best games of it's kind.
Never before have I seen a game that blends RPG and Real Time Strategy together in such a satisfying way. This is emergent gameplay at it's finest because it in no way limits you from choosing to play as you see fit. You can rise to become King of the entire world and unite them all, or undermine them all by playing them against one another in a never ending conflict, or ignore war altogether to become a trader, or a bandit, maybe even take over a castle as an illegitimate marauder and see how long you can hold out against the vast armies out to take it from you. You can travel with a huge army or a small group of interesting NPCs. Don't like the base setting? You can download mods to play in real world settings, or fantastical places like Westeros from A Song of Ice and Fire, or Middle Earth from Lord of the Rings.
If you like sandbox games, this is it at it's finest. Does it have problems? Sure, of course it does. The saving grace however is that everything else works beautifully.
COMBAT - While the AI is incredibly stupid to the point of just knowing basic "charge at you screaming" tactics and turning their back to a cavalry charge to chase one guy who broke through their lines first... the combat itself is very well done. Melee feels very intense and reactionary, you have to be on your guard at all times and be ready to take advantage of any enemy weaknesses. Archery is both deadly and difficult, and requires a serious investment for your character to be good at. Unit types are varied with no one faction sharing identical unit types. Mounted combat is the best I've ever seen in a game allowing you to use a large variety of weapons from horseback and giving serious advantage to mounted warriors. There's a lot I could say about combat but it's really got to be experienced first hand.
POLITICS - With 6 main factions in the game, rival claimants to every throne, independent troops of bandits, raiders, deserters, and the like, and the possibility to even create your own separate faction, there is a ton of variety in the game. You can side with any of the factions or none of them, you can even play several off on each other if you have good relations with multiple lords. You can marry a huge number of eligible partners, as either male or female. You can even convince certain lords to defect to your own faction if they like you well enough. You can rise in influence by doing quests, conquering enemy settlements, capturing rival lords, and defending your faction's territory.
SIEGE - Siege mechanics are a little lacking, you will only ever have one ladder (which is really a ramp) or one siege tower for any castle siege, the AI again is very basic, the archers fire from a distance but all melee and cavalry units (who dismount for the siege) just clambor up single file to the top of a wall to fight a war of numbers against a swarm of bunched together units at the top. You can issue commands to pre-defined groups (Archers, Melee, Cavalry, Etc.) to tell them where to go, what kind of weapons to use, and so on, but by and large the sieges aren't the biggest highlight though they are still incredibly intense due to awesome combat mechanics.
ROLEPLAY - While there is an element of backstory and lore to this world, mostly explored through your companion's musings on areas, by and large the world is very open for interpretation. The six factions are based off real-world equivalents like the Cossacks, Mongols, Arabs, Vikings, and Gauls both in terms of unit types and archtitecture. Roleplaying shines however in how it allows you to be whoever you want to be. You can choose to start as a lord with enough honor to have your own banner sigil, or start as a lowly thief who just runs about burning villages and trying to keep one step ahead of the law as you try and make it rich. There's so many variables that let you choose how to play the game, you can even solo the game if you want for a true challenge. There are a lot of unique stats and skills you upgrade independently that affect everything from your persuasion attemps, battle tactics, map speed, weapon skill, and the size of your army.
ACTIVITIES - Aside from combat, there are quest opportunities available in villages, towns, and from other lords who ask favors. There's maybe only 10 types of quests, that range from delivering trade goods, cattle steering, bandit hunting, village defense, soldier training, attacking enemy settlements, or capturing rival lords. In addition to this there are arenas and tournaments that allow you to bet on yourself as you fight in a host of games. Upgrading buildings in towns and villages you own. Exploring towns and castles. Attending feasts. Recruiting and training units. There's always SOMETHING to do.
Bottom line, if you haven't played this game yet and you are even remotely interested in RPGs or RTSs then you need to get it now!

Deadlight is an overlooked gem within a puddle of the overused genre that is "Zombies". The game (while being extremely short), makes up for that loss with an engrossing and believable storyline; whilst delivering impressive visuals and a generous amount of extras for the player to enjoy. Deadlights platforming is simple and concise, although at times touchy. With that being said, Deadlight comes recommended highly for the fresh and exciting gameplay that it introduces!
It only took a couple of hours to finish but its well worth it. They focused more on trying to get away then mowing everything down which is a nice change.
Watch out for ghosting on keyboard. Might actually have to play with an xbox controller. Fun game, watch out it's short.

A truly atmospheric and gripping adventure through a post apocalyptic Washington during a fictional zombie outbreak in the 1980's.
The first thing I noticed about Deadlight was how nice it looked. Being a platformer, I expected a more two dimensional approach but utilizing the Unreal Engine 3, they managed to pull off a fully 3D experience whilst retaining the old school platforming style. The lighting, animations, and effects really bring the game to life and have all been made to a very high standard.
I honestly couldn’t stop playing Deadlight at some parts. The story and characters kept me interested and I was always looking forward to the next level. The game does well to keep your interest by becoming increasingly cinematic. Flashbacks, dream sequences, strong cut scenes, all do well to make you feel like you’re part of a long film with a beginning, a middle, and an end.
There was a significant problem with Deadlight though.  I fully completed the game (with the exception of nightmare mode) over a 2 day period of about 7.5 hours. Roughly 5-6 hours in campaign length, on hard difficulty. There were parts I had to do over and over again and several areas where I just stopped and looked around.  So some people might have even beaten it in even less time. The game does warrant a second playthrough, but the Nightmare mode is proving to be too difficult for me. Playing through the entire game without any checkpoints and perma-death is balls.
So Deadlight is a great game. Solid story, interesting gameplay, and very visually appealing. I only wish they made the story that little bit longer as I didn't want it to end so soon.

It currently has 3 modes (Extraction, Escape and Hunted). Extraction is about saving other NPCs with your team, Escape about getting away from certain place (prison, for example) by finding keys, chain-cutters and so on and Hunted is where the most fun awaits, in my oppinion. It is PvP mode similar to DayZ (but much more quick-paced). Players start with a gun and a weapon and look around fairly big map for resources. They kill each other (although they also team up often) and the last one to survive wins the game.
Atmosphere is really great, sounds and easy on ears and give Contagion awesome feeling. Altought there are still trouble with hitboxes and occasional crashes, I'm having tons of fun and I can easily say that if you played Zombie Panic: Source!, you'll love this too. I got it on 75% sale and it is easily worth full price, provided developers don't stop with their hard work.

Regarding realism, this is a no-go: They somehow tried to balance the sides while giving them the same production capacity: the MG-34 has a slow firerate and costs less than the MG-42 (Which also suffers from an extremely slow firerate). On the german side, everyone starts with G-43, M1 Garand for US soldiers, and we have to buy the K-98 and M1903 rifles (80% of the price of the Mg-34)... The M1 bazooka is as effective as the Panzershreck (both pierce around 100mm, while the Panzershreck could pierce 200mm of armor. Instead of making the panzershreck less available, they equalized the two. So basically, any fan of history and realism should stop right there, these are just the tip of the iceberg.
Regarding gameplay: it could be a lot of fun with more accuracy regarding realism, but since I already spoke about that lets just jump to everything which is completely off:
When you die, you have to wait for your teammates to die (Since I try not to die, I can only imagine how horrible it has been for my teammates, I discovered this after 2 days, having to wait 5 minutes to respawn).
The game is fast, and the 'hold' objectives are usually strongly in favour of the attackers (A ratio favouring the attackers is not needed at all, you can usually kill all the defenders alone as they are parked in a 5m radius area, surrounded by lousy sandbags and scraps).
Hand to hand combat is the complete reverse: it is damn slow, and you must not be too close, else your swings will go through your intended victim without harming them. Usually, for hand to hand, you should keep your rifle unless you have the complete advantage of surprise and know you can miss if you are too close. Also you start hand to hand with spades, and have to work your way up to knives, while historically, soldiers sharpened they spades instead of their knives / bayonnets.
Tank combat is lame, you are alone in your tank, assuming driver/gunner/commander all at once. The Pz 1 a has only 25 rounds per magazine per gun (50 rounds total), and spreads its load slowly like a shotgun.
Also there's a delay between the gunscope and the gun itself... Which is completely weird given that usually, the scope is coaxial to the gun, no ?
When you see the message "armor penetrated", it doesnt mean anything, since the tanks use armor and HP, you cant kill the crewman inside his tank or damage the engine or rip out the tracks.
Regarding the "free to play feature": Well, everything in game seems to be unlockable only by playing. Which is great.
But here is the catch: Once you buy something, you can't resell it. Bugs are numerous, and you can lose money by buying several times the same item. You can change from infantryman to tankman, but you cant sell all your now useless infantryman gear. And if you revert to infantryman from tankman (costs 2.5k), you can't revert back to tankman unless you buy it again (22.5k). So if you are not deterred by the complete crappiness of the game, you should know that you have to plan in advance what you will do. If you want to be tankman, do not bother buying anything while being infantryman for example.
Also as tankman, you have to pay to repair/rearm your tank (same thing for weapons modifications as infantry). Sometimes it doesnt work and you lose all your credits.
Basically, the Free to play aspect is completely buried under the pay-to-win side, which might not be visible at first. I mean: Ok, everyone has to make a living, but it looks like the developpers were looking for nice ways to encourrage people to pay, and this part obviously turned very wrong, it might not be the worse game regarding that, but its definitely not the best.

Multiplayer:
Call of Duty: Ghosts is the 10th game in CoD series. I’ve been playing Call of Duty for 5 years now and I liked most of them. But this game is really bad. This game looks almost the same as MW2/3 which are games of more than 2 years ago. IW decided to go to take the safe path, since Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare was their biggest success, they made all prequels more or less the same. So most IW games lack innovation.
Also the amount of hackers is ridiculous. In MW2, MW3 were a lot of hackers despite the fact of the anti-cheat system IW claimed to have installed. In Black Ops 2 there was not a single hacker I encountered in the time I played the multiplayer. But after having played Ghosts one week there were already signs of wallhackers and people using aimbots. It’s really frustrating to encounter hackers after having played a game without hackers for almost a year.
Call of Duty is also infamous for their unbalanced/overpowered weapons. This time the guns are not that unbalanced however the I.E.D. makes me want to throw my computer out of the window. It is something similar to the bouncing betty but it’s hardly spottable. After you’ve heard it trigger you’re assured to explode within a few seconds. You also got a dog which has 2 times the health of a human player. It can jump on you from a distance of 5 meter and you’ll die as soon as it jumps on you. There is no animation or anything you just die instantly when he jumps.
Is there something positive about Ghosts? Why, yes there is. The maps are much bigger than in BO2. So the game won’t end up in spawnraping. But then again IW ruined it by its ridiculous spawns. For example when my team got the A and B Flag in domination and the enemy team got only the C flag there are really high chances that the enemy will still spawn at A or B. This is why using specialist or assault strike package is not recommended.
Singleplayer:
The missions in the singleplayer were okay. It could have been better but I did enjoy it for the bigger part. The missions are pretty cool and the campaign’s intro is one of the most beast intros I’ve ever played in a FPS game.
This campaign, though, is one of the easiest campaigns I’ve ever played in the CoD series. It wasn‘t much of a challenge. When you almost died you had plenty of time to run towards cover and regenerate health, even on Veteran Difficulty. There is, however, one thing I don’t like about the campaign which is the fact it has an open ending. This means IW wants to continue this series in a prequel which will probably be “Ghosts 2” or something like that. I really fear IW will make another game that is almost the same again.
Extinction:
I was really looking forwards to this new gamemode. But it wasn’t as I expected. I enjoyed playing it as long we didn’t complete the whole mission. As soon as we completed Extinction it wasn’t all that fun anymore because it became repetitive. So that’s a real shame.
Verdict: 2/10

So it's another survival zombie game.  What more is there to say?  Well, plenty actually, even for a short 3 - 4 hour length.  It's a 2.5D platformer with zombies and occasional puzzle elements, but what really stands out is the game's immersive atmosphere, both through great audio and visuals.  It also has an excellent conveyance of just how oppresive a zombie apocalypse actually can be and it's done through the game mechanics, namely the stamina meter you have to manage.  It's not all samurai swords a-swinging with rock music in the background.  Regardless of your otherwise agile main character, it's still quite exhausting fighting for your life.  Unfortunately the achievements themselves can be quite an immersion breaker, each one stupidly titled after out of place songs, including "Never Gonna Give You Up" and the endings are quite weak too.  Still, the game is likely to draw you in, and while the keyboard and mouse is functional, it feels a little awkward and I recommend using a gamepad, but that's always the case with platformers anyway.  Give it a try, I can almost promise your imagination will put you in the shoes of your main character's situation along the way.

It was divine providence that I saw this game during the Steam Summer Sale and bought it on a whim. Mount & Blade: Warband is a very addicting game.
Although the combat may look and feel clunky, it is very unique and very fun to do. The directional swinging of the sword and the blocking mechanisms seem very close to actual combat. It also feels very satisfying to get a headshot with a bow and see your enemy fall in one blow. No, even just landing a hit from a distance can make you feel accomplished, and you just strive to do even better.
The game may be a bit grindy, but the battles never get repetitive. It's all worth it if you want to achieve your goal, the main purpose of the game: to become king of Calradia. To do that, you have to first build up a big and powerful party to conquer towns and castles, and eventually kingdoms. There are different paths to reach that as well.
Of course, there will come a time when you get tired of the lack of variety in the game. No problem! There are many mods around the internet that can improve the game, and they can also completely rework the game to not make you bored again. The process is simple as well.
The graphics may not look very good, and you may end up impatient, but I guarantee that it is all worth it. I bought this game at a cheap price, but I definitely would be willing to buy it at its regular price. So go and buy it now!

Highly recommend this game if you can get it at a good price and enjoy somewhat realistic teamwork games. It is a great game in beta, its a Half life 2 mod that plays like a combination of l4d and insurgency. Its a very tactical l4d essentially, i've also heard some people compare it to the game "No more room left in hell" it has 3 differnt game modes, one being escpae, where you escape from a map and work together up to 8 people in a co-op working throughout a whole map completeing objectives to escape, there is extraction which is similar to hostage rescue in CS, instead you search houses in a nehiborhood for surivors and hold out against a zombie wave and then have the surivvors follow you, and then there is also a game mode called "hunt" which is bacialyl a deathmatch where its surivovrs vs surivors and zombies a very intresting gamestyle. Some very notable features about this game is for one it is an 8 person co-op but if you die you become a zombie and it then becomes your objective to kill off the rest of the survivors no matter what game mode your playing. This can be very anoying when playing with the general public, or if your playing with friends and members of the public it can be quite fun to go all Jones town in the very begining and work together as zombies.  The other noticable feature is the zombies are not olypmic runners, you actually can out run / manuever them which really adds a very nice elemnt of strategey as you realize you dont have to always kill every zombie, second there is some very violent animations, you shoot a zombie in the face their face gets red, you shoot them in the head (which is the only way 2 put them down I might add) brains fly onto the wall, if you shootout a zombie's kneecap they start crawling on the floor etc..It really pays off to work in a group of 3 or more people as you have 4 inventory slots and have to deicde between weapons or other items, example sometimes you may need someone to carry a fire extisingusher *♥♥♥♥ you you go ahead and spell it correctly if your so great* or bolt cutters or even keys that can unlock bonus rooms such as an armory later on in the map. You also have a cellphone that will update you on what your next objective is, or if your on extraction it works as a GPS, or if your in hunt mode it will actually beep and tell you if other players are near by. You really do need to work together in this game, and you need to conserve your ammo and take the time to line up a headshot, iron sights only and there are a variety of weapons from knifes, sledgehammers, to pistols, ak-47's AR-15's grenades even if you can find them, Tech 9 machine guns, SMGs, shotguns, hunting rifles, in some game modes you can even find a nail gun and boards and create barriers in a house by boarding up doorways and windows. very useful in extraction and hunt mode. so on a scale of 1- 10 I give this game a solid 7, Its still in beta but its got nowhere to go but up, a few minor bugs need to be fixed and some more maps added, hopefully the community will start creating some more custom maps for it and RTR will get its own private dedicated server running sometime soon. As far as the price goes most of us picked it up for $3, even at double that its worth it but as far as the asking price of $15 thats up to you I do enjoy the game but I dont know if i would pay the full $15. Best to get it while its on sale.

A typical Ubisoft game:
- Excellent graphics and visuals
- high production value in regards to storyline - voice acting etc.
- a fun adventure game
- weaponry well-rounded and accurate
- decent multiplayer
- all-round a fun and worthwhile game
unfortunately pros stop there;
- AI is unfinished. The moment that they know someone is shooting at them, they will INSTANTLY know exactly where that person is, even if they don't have "sight" (they haven't officially located you) like they will start running towards your location in an attempt to find you, even when you are a kilometer away with a silenced sniper / bow. This would be fine some of the time, but my point is it is guaranteed to happen. The only way you can not alert a gang to your precise location is to single them out when they are away from the group.
They have 100% accuracy. A sniper will always hit you, no matter how fast you are moving for example. I tested this with a trainer which allows for extrreme movement speed - even when the sniper's laser pointer was facing away from me the dude still hits me on average 0.75 shot per second, for sometimes full health. This not only feels unrealistic, but is completely unfair when an entire gang is shooting at you and they all have 100% accuracy. It makes skirmishes impossible and you are forced to take on gangs from a vast distance. even if you have cover, the moment you pop up they will all hit you and you will die unless you have fast reflexes.
for some reason you can take down enemies when they havent seen you, but you cant interact with them if they have spotted you. You have to swipe your blade randomly a couple times near them to kill them instead. So you can stand there at point blank being shot and swiping randomly, but you can't grab the dudes gun and stab him or anything like that. Feels unrealistic and cheap.
All of this makes stealth near impossible in this game, if you make a mistake you have to try all over again. You need to be 100% perfect to not get shot at.
- unoptimized for PC. Runs ok'ish, but you will find it annoying if you have a high-framerate screen. Many scenes are like 50% GPU usage at like 80fps despite vsync on and a 144hz screen. Framerate seems to depend on engine limitations, not hardware. Also physics  is dependent on FPS - above 60fps NPC's teleport, cars have odd physics and flip too easy etc.
- the physics themselves. Sick of watiting for my gun to appear after jumping onto a platform so that i can wait for the engine to reset so that the command appears to jump onto the next ledge (some ledges you can "climb" onto if you press space when the prompt appears) sometimes you can jump onto them without any prompt - although the activation for this completely illudes me. Sometimes you it will just completely fail.
Overall the physics is not by any means polished and consistent and while it is good and realistic when it works - it doesnt work all the time. It will get on your nerves.
- cannot skip any cutscenes. This is especially annoying for 2nd playthroughs. Play with -skipintro in launch commands if you dont want to sit through the unskippable intro every time you load the game up.
- button mashing and interactive cutscenes in general. Many, MANY people want these struck from all video games as do I. Make of it what you will, just saying this game has them.
- feels like an arcade game. There's no "dying" per se (you can die) but you just reset near where you were with your ammo, health, loot etc. restored. You don't have set respawn points or any consequense WHATSOEVER for dying. Makes it not feel like an open-world adventure game and more like an arcade game.
- entire game runs on storyline missions. Free roaming is limited, as are skills, as are weapons - all by storyline missions. This is fine up to a point, but the game is split into two halves. You unlock both halft the weaponry and half the map after complete the requisite missions. Again, feels like an arcade game - not an open world game.
- Actually tells you to stop killing civilians - theres no penalty for it - it just reminds you that it's not what the games wants you to do. Wtf? I thought I was on this island to do whatever I wanted?
Many more cons but I forget them. As per usual, another Ubisoft Great Idea that has been executed pretty shoddily, another game where the money has gone into advertisement, visual fidelity and voice actors rather than software engineers - it's a good video game, it's just a terrible piece of software and yet another console port (ubisoft needs to change to UbiGame).
P.S: all of this and I haven't even mentioned uPlay yet. As others have said, a completely pointless waste of customers' time. Almost ruins the game completely. We don't need more DRM for god's sakes - especiially if we buy it on Steam. Don't need two bloody launchers.
