Far Cry 3 is way overhyped and is overall a massive let down, it's a game I want to love, but suffers from so many issues and has even caused me to stop playing the game overall.
1. Difficulty, the first island was too easy, however it makes sence because it was the start of the game, however it never got harder, just easier and easier. Then the 2nd island is near impossible because the AI is broken and can see through walls, this makes stealth near impossible and missions like Doppleganger unplayable.
2. Glitches, like the mentioned AI on the second island, this game is full of glitches like clipping, Animals running around rocks, dieing from a 2ft drop and more. Looks like Ubisoft was too busy counting their pre order money instead of fixing the game as usual.
3. Weapons, like in most open world games some weapons are better then others, however Far Cry 3 is the worst when it comes to that, shotguns are useless and serve no purpose, I love shotguns, why do they have to be so sh*t in this game?
4. Boring characters, besides Vaas, all the other characters are boring and forgettable, I can't even remember who the main character is called or anyone else because they show up, bore me and then go away.
5. Boring storyline, "We were on hoilday and got kidnapped by the bad guy and I'm some chosen one who has to kill them and free people" cliche, you could predict this story so easily it's painful.
6. Multiplayer, it's dead and sadly it had really cool concepts, like sparing the MVP on the enemy team or kill him when your team won. R.I.P FC3 Multiplayer.
7. CO-OP, shoot, minigame, shoot, minigame, shoot and minigame...... fun.....
8. Skills, like most games which have skills, some are really good, some even broken and those which are awful, in Far Cry 3, 70% of all the skills I never noticed being useful, Drag someone underwater for a stealth kill? Well that's very limited and most outposts are inland and away from any water, plus I should just use A BULLET!
9. Uplay, so along with Steam, I need an even worse digital game service then Orign to play this? No thanks, when you make Orign look good, you know you f*cked up.
However there are some good things about this game.
Graphics are amazing
I love taking out outposts, it's pretty much the only reason to play this game.
Weapons are fun to use
Island is fun to explore
Crafting is fun until you get everything, then it's useless..... that sucks :c
Overall it's really flawed, but would I say is it worth the money? Wait for a sale, £15 for this is too much.

It is hard to describe a better game than Far Cry 3. It is incredibly ambitious, and hits most of what I thought it wanted to be. It's ambition lies in the depth of that island. 'That island' is where you spend the entire game, following objectives, getting involved in the story, and slowly uncovering the stories the island has told for generations past. In this way, it is very similar to the recent Tomb Raider, where a young adult from western civilization is slowly forced to devolve into an instinctual, lucky, brutal warrior. Both games also share the same "Lost" Island theme, where a slightly magical element appears in certain side missions to either enhance the gameplay or cover all the bases. Either way, I loved both games.
An important difference between these two 'movie caliber' games lies in the scripting. Tomb Raider took me on a ride, with only one direction to go, and I either had to hang on and watch, or restart when I fell off. Far Cry 3 had a simliar cinematic feel, and yet I never felt that I was on a string being led. All of my choices seemed to have consequences that didn't stop the ride, and each main mission felt fulfilling, satisfying, and advanced the story.
The missons were fantastic. As with a few of the Batman games, any quests that took place after inhaling hallucinogens were a highpoint. All of the missions could be scaled to different approaches, and nearly all could be done in unique ways. Frequently, a pirate camp had a cage with a ferocious animal locked inside. A fun way to start clearing these enemy camps was to open the cage with a sniper shot and watch through binoculars as the pirates all got together to stop the rampage. One negative, a simliar complaint with the gargoyle portions of the Batman games, is that these prison camps got tedious after awhile and luckily weren't needed to finish the story.
There were a few missons that didn't work. I was told to go and talk to Hurk as a part of every mission until the end even though he left the island early in the game. It also seemed impossible to free up an extra gun slot or fill up the skill trees in the natural progression of the game. But I loved that Far Cry 3 basically asks you if you're ready for the last mission before the finale, in case you want to bring your favorite weapons into the final cut scene. I also loved the new take on the last "rails" helicopter mission, that, for once, makes total sense based on who is flying the chopper.
Far Cry 3 also gives us the twin endings, both fitting and satisfying. I put 100 hours into this game, and I am going to miss the sense of freedom I had. I am also going to miss the possibilities; the random tiger attacking deer, the chance to pause exploring to have a knife throwing contest, and the random mysterious hidden passages sometimes set deep behind a routine pirate camp. Even though I'm done with the campaign, a part of me still wants to go back for one more look.

I have revised my earlier opinion of this game: It's got surprising depth.
TL;DR: Learn to appreciate its complexity and it's pretty cool.
Let's start with what it's not:
- Fair
- Easy
- Fast
- a TDM fest
If you expect a CoD of BF like shooter, you are mistaken. It's more like a Red Orchestra game with a campaign layer on top.
Once you make it to level 3 (which few of the reviewers have managed), you get into the real game. Troops are pitched against eachother by 'generals' in the MMO part and they have to duke it out in FPS on the battlefield. Because of the manual aspect of matching troops, one side can be horribly overpowered. While this may be a turn-off for some, I like the way every game plays differently because the mix of available units differs.
The FPS part is kind of clunky compared to modern AAA shooters, but is very playable. You either play as infantry -trying to capture or defend objectives-, tank -trying to kill anything smaller than you- or airplane -strafing and bombing the hell out of things-. While tanks and infantry are (kind of) balanced, the addition of skilled airplanes to one side may decide the outcome of the battle. Their firepower is insane and apart from some fixed AA emplacements, there is little that can be done against them.
Unlocking new items or career paths starts out painfully slow but picks up as you level up. The fact that you lose access to most unlocked equipment when you move to a new role is disheartening. Even store-bought stuff can't be transferred to a new character. You really do have to invest some gold in new characters or items if you want to hit the ground running when you start with this game.
While blasting the hell out of enemies is always cool, the real XP is in taking and defending objectives. Playing sniper in the tall grass can seem awesome, but you add little to the outcome of the game and you'll earn little XP. Soloing is a fast way back to the respawn: Stick together and work as a team. Sometimes you'll be horribly overpowered and unable to win, no matter how well you play. But nobody said war was fair.

Rating: Good. Has potential but really leans towards "hardcore" WW2 fans that have time on their hands. Play if you are ok with a relatively high grind and really wish to experience the feeling of helplessness that I am sure is associated with warfare. War is not meant to be fair, right? A very important point to address at the beginning of my review is that this game, by no means, is a Pay to win. The game, as others have stated, is a pay to avoid the grind.
The game is a very interesting take on world war two FPS/strategy and has many good features. I quite enjoy the maps and the overall layout of each level, with the environments being of excellent quality. The shooting feels a bit easier then perhaps it should be but I think the developer really tried to give a hand up to those players who want to play infantry only (you can see that easily through the relatively over durable player life). You have many options as infantry and actually can progress to becoming a recon or paratrooper soldier through playing, adding to a very fun infantry diversity. I absolutely enjoy the fact you have to work up to being a pilot or a tanker . I also love how the system regulates the number of anti tank type soldiers through randomly placed (or purchased as an add on to cars or your own tank) panzerfausts and a quite expensive rocket launcher the player can carry. I feel this does address my complaints with mainstream games such as Battlefield 3/4 where everybody and their grandmother carries some form of anti air or anti tank weapon. The game, however, has one major flaw and that is through the "steep" equipment purchasing system combined with the leveling system. I will describe that in the next paragraph where I discuss an excessive grind likely driven by a need to get the developer paid.
Game developers need to make money. Heroes and Generals is a free to play game that allows anybody with even a simple computer to play a good FPS WW2 game for free. In order to get paid, however, the development team decided to include a "gold" system allowing you to bypass the normal "credits" system that is used to buy new equipment. Gold, of course, is primarily collected through spending real world dollars (yes there are other ways but the return is quite small).  The gold system, sadly, lends this game to become like many mobile games with overly stiff "penalties" for not purchasing <insert speed token title>. A key example is in the case of selecting "tanks/armor." You begin, at least with the germans, occupying a glorified training tank with two small machine guns. You can shoot at infantry and little jeeps pretty ok but quickly realize that against anything slightly armored you are dead. So you work at this level and get blown up a few times until you reach your next level and you can purchase a new tank. Great! you get a leveling system that encourages you to play more and you get your reward, kinda.  Your reward seems decent until you realize that you need to get approximately 50k credits (or a couple hundred gold) in order to reach the slightly better level two tank that might hold it's own against something with armor.  That, depending on player ability or style, can take awhile to get.  The first couple  times you are blown up in your favoured armored class by a tank with a real gun you can say "well I'm learning"  and "well real war had horses going up against tanks and that was totally unfair." After the 30-40th time (ya I suck, ok?), however,  the game becomes work and you hear a voice over your shoulder like a little demon saying "buy the gold.. why suffer.. buy the gold." You tell the voice to go away and leer up at the horrendously steep unlock price and say "ok so I will just have to grind through this." 20-30 tanks later you now have your credit card out and you are buying the gold and feeling just a bit less proud of each accomplishment (you are not being completely destroyed anymore, however...)
Previous Review: Until  I feel that the system is not completely pushing you towards turning over your hard earned cash I cannot recommend it. I would, however, love to donate to the company/developers through a system completly separate from the game as a thanks for the hours of fun playing. I will, as per my belief, provide a review for this after another 18.6 hours of gameplay in order to be fair.
Post 36 hour review:
Summary-  Good to Play. Perhaps having to struggle and battle through things can be a good thing? You are also not a special snowflake in this game. You are not the hero but a cog in a machine (which is cool!)
So I have reached the 36 hour point with this little game and frankly, I have changed my mind. The game certainly has it's flaws, and the grinding system can be tiresome, but there are some real quality moments to the game. The graphics are fairly top notch with a steady frame rate through all events. Sounds are crisp and you, with time, can even identify particular weapons based upon their sounds (no generic shooting sounds). For a free to play game, there is no complaints here. Graphics and sounds are not everything, however, and fun and interesting gameplay is crucial to any game. I will describe that in the next paragraph.
The real hidden gem behind this game is the campaign system. The campaign system has actual experienced players selecting and allocating resources throughout a simulated europe, with each map being significantly different depending on how the "generals" value the battle. If the general fail to select appropriately, you find that you certainly fail. Hell, if the generals or commanders fail to consider multiple factors, you can easily find yourself in a half company of mechanized infantry against an army of tanks and a couple full companys of soldiers. That is tactics and your purpose, as sad as it seems, may be to simply slow the enemy. Overall, while right now the game seems slightly sided to the allies (if you have ever played star wars games you find a majority of players wish to play the "good" guys) over time I am sure quality groups and guilds will form that will really change the tides of war.
In a final statement I wish to address my original complaint about the steep grind. I originally thought the steep grind, when combined with the leveling system, was a negative to the game and often held characters back. Upon further consideration, however, I recognize how important this type of grind is to the fairness and balance of the game. I found that, at this point of the games progres, the frequency of snipers, planes, tanks, rocket launchers, and other "higher level" items are restricted to the point where you feel as if the battle was somewhat realistic. I draw a point from more blockbuster games like Battlefield 3 or 4 where, in my personal opinion, everyone has a helicopter, rocket launcher, AA gun or tank.I mean, who has not complained about a map being dominated by snipers?  To address a poitn about modern technology, I would like to say that while sure, modern warfare has seen a rapid increase in technology,  NOT every soldier (even in the US army) has some form of anti-tank anti-aa weapon. We still have squads, we still have soldiers that have just an M16 and a couple grenades.
Rating: Good. Has potential but really leans towards "hardcore" WW2 fans that have time on their hands. Play if you are ok with a relatively high grind and really wish to experience the feeling of helplessness that I am sure is associated with warfare. War is not meant to be fair, right?
What I love:
+ Campaign mode
+ Varied maps
+ Good sound quality
+ Grind system that actually slows down the acquisition of sniper rifles, planes, and tanks.
What causes me to curse:
- Slightly one sided battles with allies often victorius
- A steep grind to getting some of the better weapons
What I would love:
+Fuel and Hydraulic systems- Give a bit of realism to armor and planes with damage

This is one of my personal favourite games. The gameplay is basically Sid Meier's Pirates!, but with a medieval theme, more elaborate combat and more depth (you can earn XP to level up your character and companions, for example).
After you choose your character's background, gender and starting attributes and skills, you set out building an army and doing miscellaneous tasks for the various lords and kings of the 6 factions and mercenary work. Once you gain enough renown and a decent army, you can become a lord for any of the factions and get your own castles and cities to look after, or even create your own faction to rule over. The gameplay as a monarch in the vanilla game is a bit lacking compared to playing as a lord, but there are mods like the Diplomacy mod that elaborate on this.
The combat system is one of the most fluent i've seen in a medieval combat game. There are a varied amount of weapons, shields and weapon types to choose from, you can swing, chop or thrust your weapon by flicking the mouse and clicking and you can fight on foot or on a horse. Nothing feels delayed, there's a nice flowing feel to it and it's satisfying to kill things. Horse combat takes a while to get used to, but it's fun to charge people with a lance and to circle groups of soldiers while pouring arrows into them. It's especially fun once you get into a big 400 man battle. At times, it feels like playing a Total War game with all the soldiers running around and killing each other.
To conclude, this is an addictive game that's well worth checking out.

Mount & Blade: Warband. I could say a lot about it but I'll say a little and make it count.
I love this game.
You'll be hard pressed to find a game which gives you the thrill of riding into battle and charging the enemy lines head-on or having your archers rain hell from above as you and your cavalry pick off enemy troops from the edges of their battle lines and then sending your infantry in to charge. You have many options with this game as far as what you want to do with your character. You may either chose to fight for an established kingdom or go against the grain and dare to forge your own kingdom. The choices are yours. Their are a few downsides such as the graphics. As it is an older game, you won't see the same stunning visuals as you would from a next-gen console game. Also, like many RPG games, you'll find that many of the side quests can quickly become repetitive. The good news is that you don't have to do ANY side quests if you chose not to. There's no main story line. It's you. You are free to do whatever profession you chose to do (and there are MANY to chose from). This is one of my personal favourite games. The gameplay is basically Sid Meier's Pirates!, but with a medieval theme, more elaborate combat and more depth (you can earn XP to level up your character and companions, for example).
After you choose your character's background, gender and starting attributes and skills, you set out building an army and doing miscellaneous tasks for the various lords and kings of the 6 factions and mercenary work. Once you gain enough renown and a decent army, you can become a lord for any of the factions and get your own castles and cities to look after, or even create your own faction to rule over. The gameplay as a monarch in the vanilla game is a bit lacking compared to playing as a lord, but there are mods like the Diplomacy mod that elaborate on this.
The combat system is one of the most fluent i've seen in a medieval combat game. There are a varied amount of weapons, shields and weapon types to choose from, you can swing, chop or thrust your weapon by flicking the mouse and clicking and you can fight on foot or on a horse. Nothing feels delayed, there's a nice flowing feel to it and it's satisfying to kill things. Horse combat takes a while to get used to, but it's fun to charge people with a lance and to circle groups of soldiers while pouring arrows into them. It's especially fun once you get into a big 400 man battle. At times, it feels like playing a Total War game with all the soldiers running around and killing each other.
To conclude, this is an addictive game that's well worth checking out.

TL;DR: For anyone who is interested in the quick and dirty I do not recommend this game because of three things: Uneven Economic model, 'flawed' Matchmaking and only 'Average' FPS gameplay. However, if your interested in more grinding than a Gentleman's club then this is the game for you. Anyone else should exercise extreme caution.
With that out of the way, this is from the perspective of a relatively 'new player' so I will be wrong on some stuff.
There is also a massive disconnect between players that are mid-tier or higher in comparison to the experiences that new players are having. With generally the newer player not having much fun at all because of "reasons".
________________________________
Economics & Progression System:
It's a broken mess. The costs are simply too much for an average player / casual player to stomach.
Example 1: Let's play 'Avoid the tank!'
M1A1 Bazooka - 28,400 Credits
Corporal Salary - 1,450 Credits
You are looking at nearly 20 battles. Now, assuming that each battle lasts around 20 minutes you are looking at investing 400 minutes to buy one item. Whereas if you spend 329 gold ($2.15 assuming basic $9.16 gold package (s) of 1400 gold) you can skip that grind and actually have fun in combined arms battles.
Now this is where the first cracks appear. When you start off, you are incapable of hurting enemy tanks unless you spend RL money or nearly 7 hours grinding it out for the 'ability' to hurt enemy tanks.
This means, that until you do so, you are automatically forced into two options without it: Disengage or be killed.
This is the most painful example in the game of the broken economic model. For those first 7 hours the game is almost unbearable to play as it is simply no fun for those times that you do come up against enemy tanks. This is where I expect most players to give-up because the game has not shown there is more to it than grinding.
Example 2: You want to play the Strategy side too? Too bad. Money naow!
2nd Lieutenant Minimum - I cannot tell you how much because they don't want you to know. I'm not joking, they deliberately conceal it on their Wikia
.
You have to take me at my word here, the XP costs get so absurd that you shouldn't even try to grind this one out. You will simply be shocked at how much XP you will need to grind out in order to play with an entire half of the game. This means that your hand is being forced to pay 1,699 Gold ($11.10 assuming basic $9.16 gold package (s) of 1400 gold) in order to play with this section of the game if you have any kind of interest in advanced matchmaking, assault teams mechanics or grand strategy.
Economics & Progression Conclusion:
While it is possible to play with only a standard account and participate in lower tier missions until you are ready to take part in more advanced missions you are seriously limiting what the game has to offer. The reality is that in order get the maximum value out of your time in H&G you will need Membership status if only for the +50% credits in order to access the things that make the game cool: Weapon Mods, Vehicles, Assault Teams and that extra badge slot.
On a seperate note, in order to access an entire half of the game that has effectively been gated off with Pay Walls, you will need to spend money to play with the very cool mechanics of Assault Teams one way or another. Either through Membership or purchasing a character of that rank or higher.
________________________________
Matchmaking: Let's club some seals
Let's start off with the basics: Never touch 'Random Battle' ever. Don't do it. Ever.
If you are new to the game, for the love of gawd click 'Find Mission' and click resources. After that try to find ones that don't include tanks and aircraft. This is the beauty and the sheer horror of the matchmaking system here, new players can get into battles with seasoned veterans who have played thousands of hours and are far ahead of the curve when it comes to advancement. This is even more evident in combined-arms battles. Avoid these at all costs.
That's the problem with the matchmaker, it doesn't match you on skill or Soldier advancement. As far as I understand it's completely random and your playing with fire every time you use it.
Matchmaking Conclusion:
It's not so bad if you manually select your games so that the disparity of force between you and your fellow players is minimized. It's a lot more fun having the ability to shoot an enemy soldier rather than being forced to throw grenades at an enemy tank out of desperation.
The key problem is that there is NO explanation of the matchmaking system and what drives it in-game which shoehorns new players that don't know any better into bad gameplay experiences.
________________________________
The FPS side: 'Average' is not good, 'average' is actually bad guise
When broken down into it's core components, the FPS gameplay is merely average. I'm sorry but there's no way of going about this without hurting someone's feelings. Average is actually bad because it doesn't offer either refinement or innovation. The FPS mechanics are average that it reminds me of Battlefield 1942 from all the way back in 2004. That's not a good sign when we're talking about a game in August 2014.
Aside from a merely average FPS portion of the game, what is there for a new player to really do? Answer: Nothing. Unless you count grinding. Which I don't.
The FPS mechanics are middle of the road, meaning that they are the same as the vast majority of the rest of the other FPS' games out there. The only fundamental difference is that the lobby system for this game has some advanced mechancis that the average player doesn't have a hope of ever touching unless they pay for it.
This sameness' is exacerbated even further when you realize that there are huge problems with the game server. The entire game is basically being run on a single server and there are massive problems with hit detection. Doesn't make for the best gaming experience when your perfectly aimed shots are sliding off a target at times.
The FPS Side Conclusion:
There's nothing here we have not already seen but better. I will admit that I value Gameplay over Graphics. But the graphical fidelity of this game is on par with Battlefield 1942.
Overall Conclusion:
When you get down to the brass tacks of H&G - The concept of being able to play the strategic side and the tactical side in a Theatre of War is a very intriguing possibility but that's all it is at this point. A concept. H&G at this current stage is nothing more than a patchwork of microtransactions with a game concept slapped on. There is almost no incentive for the new player to stick around and be brow beaten for hours.
However, in the end it comes down to one important question; does the player want to spend time or money to access the one interesting part of the game - Assault Teams?

An improvement over FarCry 2.  The gameplay itself was great.  I really enjoyed the quests.  Difficulty level was quite high in taking some of the outposts (which for me is a plus).  The story was meh, and most of the characters were impossible to care about.  The measure of the game, for me, was that I played the quests frantically, hungry for a big payoff that never came.  Similar to my playthrough for another semi-open world game (The Saboteur), once I finished the storyline I never returned to find items or complete side quests.  However, in FarCry 3 the auspicious rise of the player character to more or less single-handedly wiping out the baddies is somehow even less believable in FC3 than in the Saboteaur (a petty-criminal car mechanic getting away with countless acts of sabotage and revenge against the Nazi occupation machine in Paris).  I could not get over the flawed storyline, which I think led me to feel deflated (and unwilling to pursue the open world any further) after completing it.

My first thought after an hour of playing this game was:  "Why did I put this game off for so long?!?".
Now that I've played through and finished the story for the first time, I can easily say that it's one of the top games on my list of "Go-To fun games".
The Good
-Beautiful Scenery, especially the underground Chinese city.  Just mouth dropping.  Overall one of the best looking games I've ever played with the exception of HEAVILY modded Skyrim.
-Intense voice acting, much better than the 200 words per minute FC2 voice acting.  Every character was interesting and every character sounded believable.  Well, maybe except for Dennis... he was a bit off, but everyone else was spot on.
-Stealth!  I love being able to sneak around like a ninja in games.  The sneakier a game will let me be, or the more sneaking tools a game adds, the more I like it.  The stealth here was very fun, if not very technical like the Splinter Cell series.
-Fun choice of weapons.  I would use different weapons to take down different camps.  Sometimes running and gunning with a SMG and sometimes knifing everything that moves.  Other camps were fun to just silently snipe everyone from a distant hill.
-Alligators!  The very first time I tried to cross a stream on foot an Alligator snatched me up because I totally didn't see it.  I nearly jumped out of my chair as I died horribly.
-Vaas... is the best bad guy ever.  Most people complain about cut scenes pulling them out of their games, but I looked forward every psychotic moment of interacting with Vaas.
The Bad *SPOILERS*
-Too many Lions, Tigers and Bears... not enough snakes.  It's a tropical rainforest jungle environment FHS, where are all the snakes?
-Crafting pouches.  Sorry, but hunting animal pelts to make ammo pouches was just bad.  Why in the world would I need several entire Tiger Skins to craft some strappy pouch thing?  Especially the wallet... I mean really?  I just can't find a pocket anywhere to cram a few extra dollars?  I really really have to craft a bigger alligator skin wallet to carry more money around?? Just dumb.
-Syringes were mostly useless.  I think I used two different kind of Syringes for the entire game.  Health and the Hunting Damage one for the more difficult hunting quests.
-Entirely too many sharks.  There was a lot of really cool underwater stuff going on, but the second you jump into salt water sharks start homing in on you by the dozens.
-Hunting relics.  I'm a completionist.  I like finishing every aspect of a game, but when you add 200+ stupid idols to go find in the game world, even I have my limits.
The Ugly *SPOILERS*
-Hoyt replaces Vaas for half the game.  What a bad choice.  It would be like Darth Vader dying in Episode IV and being replaced by Grand Moff Tarkin for the next two movies.  Hoyt is just not as interesting or fun to be fighting against as Vaas.  A much more interesting story would have been to build Hoyt up as this uber bad dude who turns Vaas into a psychotic animal.  Then, just when you're about to kill Hoyt, Vaas steps in and kills him instead leaving you to keep hunting Vaas.
In the end, I see Far Cry 3 as a two act play.  The first act is fun, terrifying and thrilling.  The second act is nowhere near as terrifying or thrilling, but then the game ends suddenly with a terrific bang.  What a great ending!

This game confuses me. Because it isn't badly done.
It's a f2p game, but it's mostly pay2avoidgrind. There are some p2w elements to it, but I've not noticed them have any significant impact on the game. You gain the free currency fast and unlock the gear quickly. I was in a tank with a big gun on it by my second night of playing. The interesting part is that the starter tank with a machine gun isn't actually bad. Infact, it's pretty good. You're essentially a metal box of anti-infantry that can park in any barn you want. It works well and you don't feel crapped on from above just because you're not shelling out money on unlocking upgrades quicker with real cash.
The weapons are heavily customisable and they actually make a difference. I have an SMG that fires so fast that at least one person has accused me of hacking because of it. Wonderful thing since i'm such a crap shot.
You can also steal bicycles and give people backies. Which is clearly a major selling point.
The game itself is very basic, there's not much to it. It's a WW2 shooter which feels to me like Day of Defeat on Battlefield sized maps. But it's nothing special, just a shooter.
But it has me hooked, I've no idea why. The game is average but the fact that it's a f2p game that doesn't feel like i'm forced to pay up to keep up has me smirking as i sit in my little tank gunning down anyone that comes near the cap point. I could use a bigger tank, sure. You gain currency just as quickly as you gain unlocks. But I don't want to, because everything in this game, from basic gear to bigger gear has it's place.
I'm still confused as to exactly what it is about this game I like. Maybe it's just simply because it's hitting all the right notes for a f2p game that wants to include a p2w element but doesn't feel like a monster grind or keeping me down because of it. Maybe it's because the game is barebones but feels like it has a lot of content to it and will only have more on the way?
Or maybe it's just because I can steal some American's bicycle for the glorious Fatherland.

Okay, I'm a huge World War 2 games fan and I eagerly try out all there's to play, but that doesn't mean that I just take any World War 2 game just for granted.
And that's basically how it is with "Heroes & Generals"
The idea behind this game is okay, not bad, sometimes even good.
But, the major thing that ruins this game is the heavy: "Pay to Unlock" attitude. Alright, you can earn most things through playing, but some require you to cough up serious cash. Also, the things you can unlock by just playing (Weapons, gear, etc) have to be 1st unlocked and then bought. And if you want to buy a new weapon.. Well, you better quit your day job to start and keep playing or you pay for it with real cash.
And for me, that's a serious no go. Especially if the historic content is not delivered in the correct way. Especially with weapon loadouts. e.g. The German infantry starts out with the G43 and not with the Kar98k. This is a major mistake when it comes down to following the history and standard German unit gear.
On the other hand, if you would follow history, than the Allied gear would be♥♥♥♥♥♥compared to the German weaponry. (From a technical point of view)
So, there's that, although it still doesn't feel right the way it's presented.
is it fun? Well, yes and no. It's fun because it's a new World War 2 shooter, but it sucks because there's no teamplay and the servers are pestered with spawn killers and other game play issues. (Wrong collision boxes, etc.)
If you want a nice World War 2 shooter with weapon unlocks and things the like, go play Rising Storm. It's better and runs more smooth than this "could be nice" alternative to Battlegrounds Europe Online.
And no, just because it's free, it doesn't mean you get away with just everything.

I definitely had a pretty good ride with this game. I was introduced into this series with Far Cry 4, with this being the second game I've played in the series. I've noticed a lot of similarites between the two games, in terms of gameplay and such. Regardless, I still had a lot of fun with the game as I loved Far Cry 4, so was bound to like this one as well. Solid graphics and gameplay. I don't really have much to complain about them. You have good combat as there are various ways to go with any situation, whether stealth or head on. Lots of stuff to explore and collect, side missions to do, and more. In terms of story, it serves the setting and game well. It kept me interested and wanting more. Setting is pretty good as well, taking place on an island with lots of mountains, forests, vegatation, caves, ocean, lakes, and much more. Lots to explore on this island. To be honest, I did have some mixed feelings with the last few events at the ending of the story, but overall, was satisfied and happy with the ending I chose and how it turned out. It took me about 36 hours to get 99% completion, for those wondering. I enjoyed the music of the game as well. A fair amount of times during the game's story where I thought it choice of music was quite suited and pretty cool. Overall, there's a lot to do in this game, from hunting, to racing, to assassination missions, to liberating villages, and much more. I was left pretty happy, impressed, and satisfied with this game. Would have no problem playing this game again, as I think of it to be a really great game that I'd definitely recommend to anyone. Two thumbs up from me!

I recommend it, on the merits of the amazing gameplay.  It's built on its own engine, and feels, for lack of a better way to describe it, phenomenal.  It does so much right, woodland fighting is fun, hiding behind trees, while in battlefield is almost a deathwish, offers a unique fighting experience.  Fighting in general is just crazy.  You hear the breath of your soldier, you slowly crawl across the ground with bullets flying overhead, shifting your weight from side to side.  The guns are impactful.  How do you know you've hit someone?  Not a hitmarker.  A scream.  Maybe seeing it on the killfeed at the bottom of the screen, but you might be so caught up in the battle that you miss it.  It's just extremely well put together and offers an experience that I have truly never seen before.  BUT the developers are greedy, and if a guy is willing to fork over tons of money because he has tons to spare, he can have a huge advantage.
My problem: Weapon Mods.
Yeah, they game is set and world war 2, and it has weapon mods.  The mod system is EXTREMELY well done.  Realistic.  Different bullet types, barrel types, triggers, all that seem plausible within the time period.  I've never seen a mod system done this well for a world war 2 game.
Here lies the problem.  Those mods are expensive.  And they're hardly permanent.  They degrade ludicrously fast, to the point that you pay more credits for repairing them after a round than you earn from playing that round.  So you can upgrade your springfield or kar .98 to be a one shot kill sniper, but you'll be losing money every round just for using it.  If you use "gold", the currency that is buyable with real money, you can just keep throwing money at the game and use your one-hit-kill sniper forever.
Don't get me wrong, I love the idea of being able to upgrade guns.  If you've worked for a one-hit-kill sniper and specced it out, you deserve it.  But the fact that the mods degrade is not only annoying, but not logical.  Bullets?  Okay you could run out.  But a barrel, trigger, internal part, or SIGHT being worn down to 60% durability after  going through a few clips in a battle?  It's an obvious money grab.  If it were to increase realism, maintenance costs would be minor and involve shoving a brush down your gun and oiling it.  If it were to increase balance, it wouldn't offer a serious damage advantage to anyone willing to throw tons of cash at the game.  It just makes me sick when games do this.
Weapons are expensive in the first place, but I'm okay with having to spend a lot of time for a permanent reward.  I'm used to that in free to play games.  This is horrible though, and the potential that can be squeezed out of weapons through the use of mods makes it that much worse that the only people who really use them, are the ones willing to throw money at the game to keep their durability levels up.

Mount and Blade has far exceeded my expectations.
This game has very simple graphics and fairly low specs and runs smoothly on my average PC on high graphics.
This is perhaps the best medieval simulation I have come across. It surprised me in the fact that you don't control your character in third or first person across the map, but instead you control your army as a whole in bird's-eye-view on the map.
With that perspective, you can see landmarks, villages and castles, parties of bandits, friendly and enemy armies, villagers and trading caravans passing by. Once you reach a settlement or once you get in a battle you will switch to third person where you will be able to move around and fight from horseback and on foot.
The trading and politics is surprisingly complex with different areas producing different commodities better, therfore affecting prices and relationships with each faction, town and even each individual person of interest is recorded.
This is one of the most sandbox games you can find with no real storyline or campaign. You decide what you want to achieve and become, including a bandit, trader, estate owner, aswell as various leaders of men in various factions, even the king, and then you set about to do that however you wish.
The combat is initially very challenging and will continue to be so for quite some time. The combat is also excellent fun and feels great, particularly when you can land a perfect thrust with a lance from the back of a charging horse (which is fairly difficult). Seeing your men swarm over an enemy's castle wall or charge over a hill is quite a sight.
There is plenty to play with and try to do. You could play this over and over, doing it differently each time.
I love this game, it captivated me from the start and I have spent many (far too many) hours playing it over the last 2 days.

It had to happen eventually, and for IW/Activision it couldn't have been at a worse time.
For a game that was supposed to ring in the new console generation with a bang and kick off a series to outbest Modern Warfare, Ghosts brings a sickening amount of issues, terrible design choices, and lack of innovation (even for such a stagnant series like Call of Duty).
Texture issues, random frame rate drops, lighting and shadow glitches, and even audio problems plague every inch of this game. Graphically, Ghosts looks on par if not worse than Modern Warfare 3 and somehow manages to run terribly. And why can I play the campaign on near max settings but have to revert to the lowest in the multiplayer? I don't know and I don't think IW does either.
The singeplayer campaign is nothing special, a mish-mash of the worst parts of Modern Warfare and Black Ops 2 with a healthy dose of even less "innovation" and proper storytelling and emotion than any Call of Duty game before it. The only new things this game even manages to bring to the table are the contextual lean (something not even needed on the PC version) and the freakin' dog they hyped up so much that proves to be just as much of a lame gimmick pre as post-release.
And the multiplayer - the one aspect that convinced most to crack open their wallets every year - is HORRENDOUS.
Aside from the aforementioned oddity with the online portion's graphics, all the maps save one or two are ill-designed and way too big for this kind of multiplayer game, you'll find yourself spawning amongst enemy teammates more than once a match, as of two weeks ago (when I stopped playing altogether) IW had yet to nail down hacks and exploits, the kill streak system feels gutted and useless, and the ranking/unlock system is so unnecessarily convoluted that even Call of Duty veterans will have to fumble around the menus, within menus, within menus before figuring it out.
Call of Duty: Ghosts is just a less than mediocre showing from the series and unless you absolutely, positively need your new COD fix take a pass on this one and see if next year's installment looks or is any better.

I want to like this game, I tried really hard to like this game, but it makes it really hard, if not impossible for that to happen.
Lets start with the basics, the game has a very big pay to win sort of feeling to it, you dont NEED to pay mind you, but the way the game is set up, it puts you at a big disadvantage starting out if you don't and instead try to use the ingame credits that you accrue slowly during normal play.
After that, the maps are huge. Thankfully the developers thought to include bicycles to help you get from point A to point B faster, but thats a whole nother issue I'll get to in a bit. Starting out, the maps seem big, it makes getting around a bit of a pain, but it doesn't seem too bad. You see, your first 3 ranks in the game are spent on 'training maps' or something like that, they are smaller than the average maps, but still pretty damned big. They feel comfortably sized relative to the number of players, although I think they could increase the number of players per side 50% and it would be even better. After your first 3 levels though, you go to campaign maps, and thats where it gets to be painful.
Those maps are several times larger, you NEED bicycles or apcs or cars to get around on them, otherwise you'll never see anything, however the bicycles are harder to come by on those maps, meaning you have to hoof it. Thankfully as players progress through the game they can purchase the ability to spawn cars, apc's, tanks, etc. but in my experience, its possible to end up on a server where nobody on your team has them. These maps are so large that the distance between objectives is several minutes at walking speed. That might sound cool, except at least as far as I can tell, the number of players on these maps is no greater than the smaller ones, I've yet to see more than 18 players per side, while the maps themselves are easily the size of larger 64 v 64 Battlefield style maps, it feels like the 'correct' number of players would be more along the lines of 100 per side on these actually, especially due to the fact that the maps are pretty open, meaning that players can easily spend 20 minutes going through the wilderness not seeing anyone, only to pop up behind the enemy lines and just have a good time shooting them in the back... repeatedly... nonstop. Of course, this is something that SHOULD be in the game, but the ease at which its accomplished, due to the fact that at any given time the majority of players on a team will be between their nearest spawn point and the objective they are trying to capture makes it extremely frustrating and it can and does break your momentum and just lead to a frustrated player base.
Oh, and those bicycles I mentioned? While nice in theory, they have a serious drawback in that you cannot use your weapon while riding and they make you a HUGE target. You would think that it would be an easy fix, get say 75% of the way there on bike, dismount, and hoof it for the last 30 seconds to where you're trying to go... except on these campaign maps your opponent will usually see you almost as soon as you mount the bike, and they will be firing at you, and probably kill you... and if you do manage to get to that magic 75% mark and dismount, well remember how I said that the opposing team will frequently get behind your lines? Yup, they have an uncanny knack for popping out from behind a tree 15 feet behind you and shooting you dead while you're relatively helpless for the brief couple seconds it takes to dismount.
And the other vehicles you can spawn like trucks, apcs, tanks, etc? Those are pretty cool, but again, you have to make an investment to acquire them and be able to use them, something not everyone does, and something which it doesnt seem that the matchmaking service (which is the only real way I've been able to get games... the game does let you pick your battles on the map, but ive yet to be able to get into any when i tried) takes that into account, as i've played on these larger maps where one side was almost entirely devoid of these vehicles, meaning they were forced to walk where bicycles weren't available. In fact, it gets worse, as it doesn't even attempt to balance the number of players with access to things like tanks against eachother. I am writing this, after having just completed a game in which the opposing team had not one, not two, but THREE tanks (mixture of Shermans and Hellcats) against my own teams ZERO, we had nothing larger than a Kubelwagen armed with a machine gun, which is effectively useless against heavy armored vehicles like the ones we were up against.
Theoretically this is counteracted by the fact that players can equip themselves with things like panzerschrecks, bazookas, anti-tank mines, etc. but there are two problems with this - the first is that as far as I know this isn't possible DURING a battle, you have to have your loadout, etc. set up before the battle, the second issue is that access to these weapons is a function of both your rank and how much you're willing to pay. Yes, of course you can use the in-game currency to buy a panzerschreck instead of paying out of pocket, but its not really something you want to spend your credits on, as doing so means that you're not spending money on new rifles or weapons modifications, etc. Beyond that, equipping that panzerschreck occupies an equipment slot, which one im not sure, because I (like most it seems) haven't purchased a panzerschreck, which means - theoretically speaking - that you could end up equipping that weapon and ending up on a map where you have no real targets to use it against (I certainly haven't seen tanks very often, and the lighter vehicles like jeeps are easily handled with small arms).  The developers DID however seemingly have the foresight to provide the spawn areas with panzerfausts (and presumably a LAW type weapon for the allies), however that has yet to materialize as a viable solution in the games I've played. Picking up the panzerfaust means you have to carry the panzerfaust, as in it replaces your rifle, so when you inevitably encounter enemy infantry BEFORE you get close enough to actually be able to get a shot off at the enemy vehicle your options are to fire the panzerfaust at them in the hopes that you kill them, or drop the panzerfaust to pull your rifle back out, you'll often be killed before you can manage that. On top of that, the panzerfaust is rarely a one hit kill unless its one of the lighter vehicles like the jeep, and given that its a single fire weapon, that means that firign at the enemy tank won't kill it or necessarily even neutralize it, just damage it, so unless one of your other teammates managed to pick up a panzerfaust (its often not very easy to find), somehow survive long enough to get into engagement range and fire it off, chances are your opponents will have the tank repaired before you have a second shot.
Which brings me to my next issue with the game, cover. I love that the game requires you to move tactically to be successful, running in the open WILL GET YOU KILLED. Thats a good thing, I think. The problem is that crouching is terribly slow, and for all the open space on these maps, it will take you a REAL long time to get around that way. And dont even get me started on prone, it might make you harder to spot and hit, but it also makes you effectively defenseless, as you move unrealistically slow, and actually turning around while prone is evidently impossible, so if you need to see whats behind you... yeah, you're going to have to stand back up. On top of that, moving tactically is largely useless when your opponents are just as likely to be behind you as they are in front of you. Most of my deaths come from being shot from my side or rear, likewise most of the kills I have come from shooting someone from the side or in the back, even when I'm in a 'head-on-head' engagement. Anyway, thats all the character limit will allow me to say.

For a game that is still in Beta, Heroes and Generals  is quite an impressive addition to the fps genre. Unlike other shooters like Call of Duty, there is no way to win in this game without teamwork. There is no team deathmatch. You have to work with your team to seige and defend objectives, and you earn victory progress by controlling more objectives than the enemy.
The combat is gritty, thrilling, and realistic. Odds are if you are not being careful and staying in cover as much as possible, you will be shot. There are controllable fighter planes, bombers, bicycles, motorcyles, civilian vehicles, armored cars, and tanks. The graphics are great and can be easily adjusted in game, just make sure your graphics driver is updated to the most recent version. When I updated my Nvidia driver, my fps jumped from ~25 to 50 with the same settings.
H&G is  so far a great game, and I expect to get many hours of competitive fun out of it, and as a bonus, the game is currently free, so there is no harm in trying it out.

Mount and Blade has far exceeded my expectations.
This game has very simple graphics and fairly low specs and runs smoothly on my average PC on high graphics.
This is perhaps the best medieval simulation I have come across. It surprised me in the fact that you don't control your character in third or first person across the map, but instead you control your army as a whole in bird's-eye-view on the map.
With that perspective, you can see landmarks, villages and castles, parties of bandits, friendly and enemy armies, villagers and trading caravans passing by. Once you reach a settlement or once you get in a battle you will switch to third person where you will be able to move around and fight from horseback and on foot.
The trading and politics is surprisingly complex with different areas producing different commodities better, therfore affecting prices and relationships with each faction, town and even each individual person of interest is recorded.
This is one of the most sandbox games you can find with no real storyline or campaign. You decide what you want to achieve and become, including a bandit, trader, estate owner, aswell as various leaders of men in various factions, even the king, and then you set about to do that however you wish.
The combat is initially very challenging and will continue to be so for quite some time. The combat is also excellent fun and feels great, particularly when you can land a perfect thrust with a lance from the back of a charging horse (which is fairly difficult). Seeing your men swarm over an enemy's castle wall or charge over a hill is quite a sight.
There is plenty to play with and try to do. You could play this over and over, doing it differently each time.
I love this game, it captivated me from the start and I have spent many (far too many) hours playing it over the last 2 days.

If you are thinking of buying this game but the dated graphics mean a deal breaker for you, then you are about to commit the biggest mistake of your life.
This is one of the best medieval combat/strategy games I have ever played.
If you’ve ever wanted to experience what it must have felt like to lead a group of men into battle to further your ambitions then this is the game for you.
You customize everything about your character including his or her physical features as well as his or her background and skills, and then quickly set off on your adventure. You’re a nobody at first and very few but the most desperate are willing to flock to your banner and cause but that quickly begins to change as you slowly but surely begin to make a name for yourself in Calradia. You get the freedom to play however you want, from becoming the loyal vassal to the king of one of the many countries in the game to a rogue bandit lord pillaging and burning his way trough everyone that crosses your path, eventually carving your own country out of blood and steel.
The combat is amazing, and very responsive. It all takes place in third person so you can lead your men and fight from the front line. It might take you a little bit to get used to it since it has a bit of a curve, but once you learn it it’ll be the richest experience you’ll have.
There’s a ton of community support and mods for it that are extremely varied.
You can play a mod that adds a fantasy element, a mod that lets you play as a common soldier that joins up with a Lord’s army and fight for him, a mod that turns the game into the Crusades or lets you lead your own Roman Legion, or fight in Japan during the samurai era.
My personal favorite has got to be the Game of Thrones: Clash of King’s mod that drops you into George R.R Martin’s Westeros during the War of the Five Kings. You can recruit men from any of the seven kingdoms or across the Narrow Sea and pledge your loyalty to any of the houses playing the game of thrones.
It’s a great game, and I cannot recommend it enough, if you’ve ever wanted to experience leading men into battle in the middle ages, feeling the exhilaration of storming a castle and putting each of it’s defenders to the sword, going from being an orphaned gutter rat to the king of the entire continent then this is the game for you.

Honestly, i've been looking for a game like this for a while. I have spent way too long playing modern warfare type shooters, and seeing ww2 starting a comeback into the games market has been a refreshing breath of fresh air. While it has its faults, one should keep in mind that this is still in beta, and bugs are to be expected.
The gameplay itself is interesting, with it being split into two parts- the heroes, which plays like a blend of red orchestra 2 and battlefield, sitting somewhere in the middle, and the generals aspect, which plays as a real-time strategy game. However, whatever the generals do in terms of sending resources affects the people playing the "heroes" part of the game. This interesting twist on the classic fps provides an extra sense of depth to the game, giving even more freedom as to how you the individual want to play it.
There are a few things the devs could add to perfect this- more maps, or a destructible environment for instance. The game itself is a work in progress however, and we could see such updates in the future.
Overall, I would give the game a solid 8/10, perhaps bordering on a 9. The new ideas and features in the game help it to break away and set itself apart from other free to play and first person shooter games,and will hopefully help to bring ww2 back as a viable genre into the gaming community.

I have mixed feelings about my time playing Far Cry 3: I can’t say I didn’t enjoy it, but I was
repeatedly frustrated throughout my fifty-hour experience. It could have been so much more;
it just needed a lot more polish.
The game is set on a fictional, tropical island where Jason Brody, the character you play, is
stranded after escaping captivity. For the course of the game you fight a group of pirates led
by the central antagonist, a megalomaniac called Vaas, who has captured your friends and
is holding them prisoner.
As far as I’m concerned this is as much as the story has to offer: it lacks originality and good
writing, and the plot is contrived to say the least. The trouble is that hidden underneath the
story is a series of fetch quests that lead your character from one location to the next. Whilst
in moderation this can be a good design technique; it’s at odds with the fact you’re
undeniably a badass: It just doesn’t make sense for you to run around playing fetch when
instead you could cut the crap, and kill the bad guy(s).
The cutscenes are also all too frequent and unescapable: there is no way to skip them. I
found myself continuously bringing up the Steam interface to entertain myself, while they
were playing in the background. The majority of characters are cliché, with poorly written
lines of dialogue and wooden voice acting; the one exception being Vaas, whose character
is well written and genuinely intimidating.
My other major gripe with the game is the number, and repetitiveness, of the bland side
quests: they really feel as if they have been added for the sole purpose of extending the
game. This seemed pointless to me, and I deliberately avoided completing them, although I
did enjoy capturing all of the outposts (enemy bases held by the pirates) spread across the
island.  It is a good opportunity to test out the weapons you unlock, and to experiment with
the excellent stealth system.
Having said all this, if you ignore the story, there are a number of aspects that are really
enjoyable. The graphic fidelity is excellent, textures are sharp and the lighting is
breathtaking. At maximum settings you enjoy a large view distance, with few textures
popping in, and the topographical design of the island is truly beautiful to behold. Although I
did have a number of performance related issues, with frame rates occasionally dropping
below sixty without any obvious reason, despite running with GTX 970’s in SLI.
The crating system, although contrived, is still entertaining: I enjoyed seeking out, and
hunting, the different animals required to craft upgrades for your character. The number and
variety of animals inhabiting the island is really quite staggering; from sharks to tigers, the
whole variety of top predators is, literally, at your disposal (or quite often, theirs).
The variety and feel of the weapons is also excellent; I can’t think of any recent game which
has the same selection and customisation options. Almost all of the weapons can be
customised with a variety of attachments: silencers, scopes and extended magazines to
name a few. It really helps to make up for the frustrating story and repetitive side quests,
adding considerably more depth and playability to the game.
Far Cry 3 is not a bad game: it’s just not a great game. I had fun playing it, but I also felt
obliged to finish it, making it difficult to recommend. If you enjoy freedom, lots of weapon
choice and customisation, and you are not bothered by a poor story, there is plenty here for
you to experience. However if, like me, you have an enormous list of games to get through,
and you want to experience the very best that the industry has to offer, I would look
elsewhere.

If you are thinking of buying this game but the dated graphics mean a deal breaker for you, then you are about to commit the biggest mistake of your life.
This is one of the best medieval combat/strategy games I have ever played.
If you’ve ever wanted to experience what it must have felt like to lead a group of men into battle to further your ambitions then this is the game for you.
You customize everything about your character including his or her physical features as well as his or her background and skills, and then quickly set off on your adventure. You’re a nobody at first and very few but the most desperate are willing to flock to your banner and cause but that quickly begins to change as you slowly but surely begin to make a name for yourself in Calradia. You get the freedom to play however you want, from becoming the loyal vassal to the king of one of the many countries in the game to a rogue bandit lord pillaging and burning his way trough everyone that crosses your path, eventually carving your own country out of blood and steel.
The combat is amazing, and very responsive. It all takes place in third person so you can lead your men and fight from the front line. It might take you a little bit to get used to it since it has a bit of a curve, but once you learn it it’ll be the richest experience you’ll have.
There’s a ton of community support and mods for it that are extremely varied.
You can play a mod that adds a fantasy element, a mod that lets you play as a common soldier that joins up with a Lord’s army and fight for him, a mod that turns the game into the Crusades or lets you lead your own Roman Legion, or fight in Japan during the samurai era.
My personal favorite has got to be the Game of Thrones: Clash of King’s mod that drops you into George R.R Martin’s Westeros during the War of the Five Kings. You can recruit men from any of the seven kingdoms or across the Narrow Sea and pledge your loyalty to any of the houses playing the game of thrones.
It’s a great game, and I cannot recommend it enough, if you’ve ever wanted to experience leading men into battle in the middle ages, feeling the exhilaration of storming a castle and putting each of it’s defenders to the sword, going from being an orphaned gutter rat to the king of the entire continent then this is the game for you.

I've come back to this many times. Maybe that's a sign of it being a good game, but I think that it's really just that it has a lot of wasted potential. Basically, the biggest problem is that more expensive weapons are just better. Significantly better, and you'll be pitted against them constantly once you've played more than a couple of hours. It's a fun game when everyone is on the same playing field. But without any type of MMR, if you aren't good at this game, or even if you don't have good weapons, expect to get uneven matches. I mean, the disparity between weapons is insane. The basic SMG you have has a huge dispersion, and is only good at short ranges. You play this game for a hundred hours, and you can get an LMG that has a similar dispersion, but only when hip firing, and does an insane amount of damage. That's just not a fair fight. Even when you do get a decent weapon, expect to grind with it for hours to get the upgrades to make it good. I mean, a Mosin-Nagant goes from 50 damage to 100. That's huge. Guides recommend that only experts play without all of the upgrades you can get. But you need to play the game for so long to get those upgrades.

Far cry 3 is the third game in the franchise, not related at all with previous games but always with the same theme , being alone in an island trying to survive.
In this game you're jason brody a spoiled teenager with a rich family who went on an adventure with his friends and ex girlfriend until one day they heard about this island where there's no laws, little did he know it would change his life forever, now he has to rescue his friends from the pirates and Vaas with the help of the Rakyat people who are trying to make a warrior out of him.
The gameplay is quite solid you can go full stealth with knife and silenced weapons, even a bow , or you can go guns blazing with rocket launchers, shotguns and assault rifles , everytime you do something in the game like capturing an outpost or exploring the land you get experience to unlock new skills like better sprint, double takedown, etc.
During your travels you will meet interesting characters who you might have to work with or against them in order to search for your captive friends.
There's a lot of side quests to do in the game, some are the trials of the rakyat which are assasination missions, hunt missions, and more.
Everytime you kill a wild animal you can gather it's skin in order to craft more ammo pouches, be able to carry more weapons,craft syringes from plants and more.
There's also a co-op mode where you explore the story of 4 characters totally unrelated to the main campaign and player vs player matches online.
This game is a must buy even at 30$, the only downsides are the double DRM you need uplay to play, and how you can be almost immortal by late game. |

I almost gave up on this game before it even really began.  The first mission, which is a "sneak" mission, was extremely sour to me.  I do not like sneak missions (there are two of them in this game), and I put the game down twice before finally picking it back up and actually getting into the actual game.  However, as one can see, I'm recommending the game.  I actually give it somwehere around a 6.5 on a 10 scale.  It does a lot of things really well, and I played all the way through to the end.
I'll start with the bad.  What I commonly refer to as "play control" really sucks.  I mean, it's terrible.  There is nothing like being stuck in the middle of a firefight, running for cover, and getting stuck on an unseen object on the ground.  A lot of the time, mission updates will appear at the top left corner, but I'm in the middle of some crazy action.  It's easy to miss these updates because of that.  There were also a lot of missions that I flat out didn't like.  The weird hand-to-hand combat screens against bosses were stupid.  Plus, the end was very anti-climactic.
However, it did a lot of things well, too.  The "treasure hunting" part of the game which involves searching for relics, letters, and disk drives was not too extensive.  It was actually just right.  When I completed all of the side missions, I felt like I had accomplished something.  It was exactly the right amount of challenge.  The "levelling system" was kind of unorthodox, and while I didn't exactly think it was the greatest, it kept me interested.  The actual length of the game was also just about right.  I put in about 54 hours, but I completed all of the side quests.  The voice acting was exceptional as well.  The plot lacked just a little bit to be desired, and I'll get into that.  I must preface that with a spoiler alert, though.
***SPOILER ALERT****
There are two protagonists in this game.  The first one is a baddie named Vaas.  I really liked him as a bad guy.  He was the right amount of crazy.  I have two problems with the plot, though.  First and foremost, Vaas kept capturing me, and I kept getting away.  How stupid is that?  He kept doing stupid things like lighting a building on fire or pushing me into a lake with a weight attached.  I mean, why doesn't he just kill me already?  Secondly, when Vaas does finally bite it, I felt like the game's plot was pretty much over.  The "second plot", where I have to go kill Hoyt, just seemd like it was only realy extending the game.  Perhaps they could have introduced Hoyt sooner to make it seem like the second half of the game wasn't so contrived?
All in all, it was a good game.  I don't know if I'll play Far Cry 4 or not.  This one was just the right length.

Far Cry 3 is the best/worst game you will ever play.
It gives you a wide open world to explore at your pace, but only when it suits the game
It gives you plenty of side missions to complete in your own way, but they all have arbitrary rules that you need to follow.
It gives you a gripping story of a dudebro trapped on an island who lets go and makes his own way, losing his sanity in the process.
At the same time you will lose your sanity because while your free to do whatever you want, you can only be as free as the game lets you.
For examply, for arbitrary reasons the game restricts your progression until you've completed certain missions. Theres no real reason listed in the plot. Theres no gameplay stability that is disrupted in the gameplay that letting you level up however you want. The game has no reason to restrict you.
But it does.

Far Cry 3 is an open world first-person shooter published by Ubisoft Entertainment. It is the next installment of Far Cry series after Far Cry 2.
Far Cry 3 gameplay, it has open world, it has small RPG element, and it has one of the best villain character ever. In my opinion Far Cry 3 open world feature is almost similar to Assassin's Creed where you have to climb a radio tower, interact some sort of panel to explore some area on the world around the tower. In Far Cry 3 you don't just get to shoot somebody and run. You can buy and upgrade weapons in store, level up getting new tattoos which conveniently giving you new abilities such as walk faster or something, also, there are some upgrades that require you to hunt for animals hide or plants. The best part is, when you shoot a tiger, it will fight back! Let your guard down and a leopard will eat you. Got bored? Maybe you should go to a village and play some poker games and rob those poker players. Do you want to become Hawkeye? Legolas? or maybe Rambo? Use explosive archer and blow some goats. Got angry? Use a flamethrower and burn the forest! Far Cry 3 has many great feature for a first-person shooter. You will like it.
Far Cry 3 has cool graphics, it is one of the best graphics I've ever seen, not because its so advanced, but because the weapons first-person animation is unique, so alive and... Okay maybe it's not one of the best, but I like it. Far Cry 3 has very good performance.
Too bad Far Cry 3 multiplayer feels like it has been left out, because it's not as awesome as the singleplayer mode. I was thinking the multiplayer will be more like huge maps on the same island, hundreds of players fighting together, something like that. Same thing about the cooperative play. But at least you get to blow something up with bow in singleplayer.
Far Cry 3 is not bad, its good, I recommend this.

Mount & Blade: Warband is a fun and interactive sandbox game with the world to explore and conquer. Starting out as lowly mercenary, or if you choose the easy route as a noble, you build your way up to kingly status. A great game for those who like lots of action, such as gamers who play FPS games, because of the large variety of melee and ranged weapons. There is as much strategy as there is close-up action, so have a quick thinking mind if you don't want to get robbed in this game. Some slight glitches (for example: one AI Lord can loot an entire village), and lots of frustration from time to time, but that is what makes the game challenging.
